name: Equities
blurb: How equity is issued, owned, traded and valued: from share classes, voting and liquidity to DDM, FCF, residual income, multiples, forecast models and CAPM-based cost of equity. The 2027 version is almost entirely new and leans hard on valuation and forecasting.
accaNote: FM gives you the Gordon growth/dividend valuation model, P/E valuation, CAPM with a given beta and rights issues; BT/SBL give you Five Forces and PESTEL. Almost everything else here (voting mechanics, float and ADV, FCFF/FCFE/RI, justified multiples, forecast models, research reports, beta regression and factor models) is new.

modules.title: Equity Instrument Features
modules.summary: What a share actually gives you: a residual, perpetual, limited-liability claim. Covers common vs preferred shares, their add-on features, other equity-linked instruments, and publicly listed vs private equity.

acca.note: FM covered ordinary vs preference shares as sources of finance. New for CFA: the investor-side vocabulary (cumulative, participating, callable/putable preferred), equity-linked instruments, and the public vs private equity comparison.

lessons.title: Common and preferred shares

cards.title: What common equity is
cards.body:
Common shareholders own the **residual claim**: they get what is left after creditors and preferred holders are paid, both each year (earnings) and in liquidation.

Key features:
- **Perpetual**: no maturity date
- **Limited liability**: you can lose only what you invested
- **Discretionary dividends**: no legal obligation to pay
- **Voting rights**: usually elect the board and approve major changes

Residual claim = highest risk in the capital structure, so the highest required return.

cards.title: Preferred (preference) shares
cards.body:
Preferred shares sit **between debt and common equity**. They pay a fixed dividend that must be paid before any common dividend, and rank ahead of common in liquidation.

But: missing a preferred dividend is **not a default**, preferred holders usually have **no vote**, and the upside is capped. They behave like a perpetual bond with weaker protection.

Risk order (lowest → highest): secured debt → unsecured debt → preferred → common.

cards.title: Preferred share features
rows: Missed dividends accrue (arrears) and must be paid before any common dividend
Extra dividends if profits exceed a threshold; may share in liquidation surplus
Holder can swap into common shares
Issuer can redeem at a set price
Holder can sell back at a set price

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body:
Ask **who owns the option**. If the holder owns it (convertible, putable), the share is worth more than an otherwise identical plain preferred. If the issuer owns it (callable), it is worth less, because the issuer calls exactly when rates fall and the share would have been worth more.

Also: cumulative protects the holder from skipped dividends; it does not guarantee they will ever be paid.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM taught preference shares from the **issuer's** side (cost of finance, K_{p} = D/P_{0}). CFA asks from the **investor's** side: which features add or remove value, and where each claim ranks. Same instrument, flipped lens.

lessons.title: Equity-linked instruments; public vs private equity

cards.title: Other equity-linked instruments
cards.body:
- **Warrants**: long-dated call options issued by the company; exercise creates new shares (dilution).
- **Rights**: short-dated options given to existing holders to buy new shares, usually below market price, to protect against dilution.
- **Convertible bonds**: debt that can be swapped into shares.
- **Depositary receipts (DRs)**: certificates traded in one market representing shares of a foreign company held by a custodian bank (e.g., ADRs in the US, GDRs elsewhere).

cards.title: Types of private equity
cards.body:
- **Venture capital**: minority stakes in early-stage, high-growth firms.
- **Leveraged buyouts (LBOs)**: buy a mature company mostly with debt; a **management buyout** (MBO) is when existing managers are the buyers.
- **Private investment in public equity (PIPE)**: a listed company sells a block of shares privately, often at a discount, when it needs capital quickly.

Companies go private to escape reporting costs and short-termism; they go public to raise capital and give owners liquidity.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Public equity's advantages (liquidity, transparency, price discovery) are private equity's disadvantages, and vice versa. Private owners gain control and freedom from public reporting but give up liquidity, which is why they demand higher expected returns.

questions.stem: Compared with common shares, preferred shares most likely:
options: have a higher claim on assets in liquidation
carry stronger voting rights
offer greater upside if earnings grow strongly
questions.explanation: Preferred shares rank ahead of common shares in liquidation and for dividends. They usually have no (or limited) voting rights, and their fixed dividend caps the upside, so the other two describe common shares, not preferred.

questions.stem: Holding all else equal, which preferred share is most likely to be worth the least to an investor?
options: Cumulative, putable
Non-cumulative, callable
Cumulative, convertible
questions.explanation: Non-cumulative means skipped dividends are lost, and callable gives the issuer an option to redeem when it suits the issuer. Both features reduce value to the holder. Cumulative, putable and convertible features all protect or benefit the holder.

questions.stem: A company has not paid its cumulative preferred dividend for two years. Before it pays any common dividend, it must:
options: obtain preferred shareholders' approval through a vote
pay only the current year's preferred dividend
pay all preferred dividends in arrears plus the current preferred dividend
questions.explanation: With cumulative preferred, unpaid dividends accumulate as arrears. All arrears and the current preferred dividend must be paid before common shareholders receive anything. Paying only the current year would apply to non-cumulative preferred; no vote is required.

questions.stem: A participating preferred share differs from a plain preferred share because it:
options: may receive dividends above the stated rate when profits exceed a threshold
accrues missed dividends as arrears
can be converted into a fixed number of common shares
questions.explanation: Participating preferred shares receive the fixed dividend plus a share of extra profits (and sometimes liquidation surplus) above a set threshold. Conversion describes convertible preferred; accrual of missed dividends describes cumulative preferred.

questions.stem: Compared with investing in publicly listed equity, investing in private equity most likely involves:
options: greater liquidity and lower required returns
less public disclosure and lower liquidity
continuous market pricing and short holding periods
questions.explanation: Private equity is illiquid, has limited public disclosure and is valued by periodic appraisal, so investors demand an illiquidity premium. Greater liquidity and continuous pricing describe listed equity.

questions.stem: A listed company that needs capital quickly sells a block of new shares directly to a few institutional investors at a discount to the market price. This is best described as a:
options: rights offering
leveraged buyout
private investment in public equity (PIPE)
questions.explanation: A PIPE is a private sale of a public company's shares to selected investors, typically at a discount. An LBO is a debt-funded acquisition of a whole company. A rights offering is made to all existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

questions.stem: A US investor wants to own shares of a Japanese company but prefers to trade in US dollars on a US exchange. The most suitable instrument is a(n):
options: American depositary receipt
warrant
rights issue
questions.explanation: An ADR is a dollar-denominated certificate traded in the US that represents shares of a foreign company held by a custodian bank. A warrant is a company-issued call option; a rights issue is an offer of new shares to existing holders.

questions.stem: Which statement about common equity is most accurate?
options: Common shareholders are entitled to a fixed dividend that ranks ahead of preferred dividends.
Common equity has no maturity date and shareholders' losses are limited to their investment.
Failure to pay a common dividend is an event of default.
questions.explanation: Common equity is perpetual and carries limited liability. Common dividends are discretionary and rank after preferred dividends, and skipping a dividend (common or preferred) is not a default.

questions.stem: Market interest rates fall sharply. Compared with an otherwise identical non-callable preferred share, a callable preferred share will most likely:
options: fall in price, because the call feature becomes more valuable to the holder
rise in price by more, because its dividend is now above market rates
rise in price by less, because the issuer is likely to redeem it at the call price
questions.explanation: When rates fall, the non-callable share's value rises freely. The callable share's value is capped near the call price because the issuer will redeem it, so it rises by less. The call option belongs to the issuer, so it gains value for the issuer, not the holder.

questions.stem: When warrants issued by a company are exercised, the most likely effect is that:
options: existing shareholders are diluted because new shares are issued
the company's share count is unchanged because existing shares are delivered
the company pays cash to the warrant holders
questions.explanation: Company-issued warrants are exercised by paying the exercise price for newly issued shares, which increases the share count and dilutes existing holders. The company receives cash; it does not pay it.

questions.stem: Relative to private equity, the main advantage of publicly listed equity for a company's founders is most likely:
options: freedom from mandatory public disclosure
the ability to sell their shares more easily
less pressure from short-term earnings expectations
questions.explanation: Listing gives founders liquidity: a market where they can sell shares. Freedom from public disclosure and less short-term pressure are advantages of staying private.

flashcards.back: Residual claim; perpetual (no maturity); limited liability; discretionary dividends (plus voting rights).
Cumulative: missed dividends accrue as arrears and must be paid before any common dividend. Non-cumulative: missed dividends are lost.

flashcards.front: Callable vs putable preferred: who gains?
flashcards.back: Callable: option owned by the issuer → lower value to holder. Putable: option owned by the holder → higher value to holder.
Receives the fixed dividend plus extra dividends when profits exceed a threshold (and may share liquidation surplus).
Warrant: long-dated call issued by the company. Right: short-dated option for existing holders to buy new shares (often below market) to avoid dilution.
Certificate traded in one market representing shares of a foreign company held by a custodian bank.
Private investment in public equity: a listed company sells shares privately to selected investors, usually at a discount.

modules.title: Equity Jurisdictions, Classes, and the Voting Process
modules.summary: How economic rights (cash flows) and voting rights (control) vary across share classes and countries, and how the shareholder vote actually works: management, board, proxy advisors, asset managers and asset owners.

acca.note: SBL covered corporate governance, boards and institutional investor stewardship in general terms. New for CFA: dual-class structures, statutory vs cumulative voting arithmetic, jurisdiction differences, and the mechanics of proxy voting and who influences it.

lessons.title: Economic rights, voting rights and share classes

cards.title: Two bundles of rights
cards.body:
Each share carries:
- **Economic rights**: dividends, residual claim in liquidation, and often **pre-emptive rights** (first chance to buy new shares to avoid dilution).
- **Voting rights**: elect directors, approve mergers, auditors, charter changes and (in many markets) executive pay.

The default is **one share, one vote**. Share classes break the link: control and cash-flow rights can be separated.

cards.title: Dual-class and multiple share classes
cards.body:
A **dual-class** structure gives one class (often held by founders) several votes per share, while public investors hold low- or no-vote shares.

Example: Class A = 1 vote, Class B = 10 votes. Founders owning 20% of the equity in Class B can control a majority of votes.

Pros: protects long-term vision, deters hostile bids. Cons: entrenchment, weaker accountability; investors often apply a discount. Some index providers restrict or underweight low-vote shares.

cards.title: Statutory vs cumulative voting
cards.formula: Shares needed to guarantee k seats = k × S ÷ (N + 1) + 1
cards.note: Statutory: votes per seat = shares held, so a majority wins every seat. Cumulative: votes = shares × N, which can all go to one candidate.

cards.title: Cumulative voting example
cards.body:
10 million shares vote; 4 directors are elected. You own 2.5 million shares.

**Statutory**: 2.5M votes per seat vs 7.5M for the majority → you win **0** seats.

**Cumulative**: you have 2.5M × 4 = 10M votes to concentrate. One seat needs 10M ÷ 5 + 1 = 2,000,001 shares → you guarantee **1** seat. Two seats need 4,000,001 shares.

cards.title: Jurisdictions differ
cards.body:
- **US/UK**: dispersed ownership; one share, one vote is common, but US tech firms often use dual-class.
- **Continental Europe**: controlling families and **loyalty shares** (e.g., double votes after holding for a minimum period, as in France).
- **Japan**: cross-shareholdings among related companies, now being unwound.
- **China**: A-shares (onshore), H-shares (Hong Kong); state ownership common.

Concentrated ownership shifts the key conflict from managers vs shareholders to **controlling vs minority** shareholders.

lessons.title: The voting process and who influences it

cards.title: How a vote happens
cards.body:
1. Management and the board set the agenda for the **annual general meeting** (or a special meeting).
2. A **record date** fixes who may vote.
3. A **proxy statement** (notice of meeting) describes each resolution and the board's recommendation.
4. Most holders vote by **proxy**: they instruct someone else (often electronically, via intermediaries) to vote for them.
5. Votes are counted; some resolutions are binding (director elections, mergers), others **advisory** (e.g., say-on-pay in many markets).

cards.title: Who does what
rows: Prepares proposals and proxy materials; runs the company
Represents shareholders; recommends how to vote; oversees management
Research resolutions and issue voting recommendations (e.g., ISS, Glass Lewis)
Vote the shares they manage on clients' behalf; stewardship and engagement
Pension funds, insurers, endowments: own the votes; set voting policy or delegate

cards.title: Shareholder proposals and engagement
cards.body:
Shareholders meeting ownership thresholds can file **shareholder proposals** (e.g., on board independence, climate disclosure). Investors also **engage** privately with management before using their vote.

If engagement fails, options include voting against directors, filing proposals, a **proxy contest** (nominating rival directors) or simply selling the shares ("voting with your feet").

cards.title: Issues in the system
cards.body:
- **Proxy advisor influence**: many funds follow recommendations closely; critics cite one-size-fits-all policies and conflicts of interest.
- **Separation of ownership and voting**: asset managers vote, but asset owners bear the economic outcome. **Pass-through voting** lets end investors choose.
- **Securities lending**: lent shares carry the vote to the borrower; lenders must recall shares before the record date to vote.
- **Index funds** hold large stakes but cannot sell, so voting and engagement are their main levers.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: SBL treated institutional investors and stewardship as governance concepts. CFA expects you to know the **mechanics**: record date, proxy, binding vs advisory votes, the different roles of proxy advisors vs asset managers vs asset owners, and the cumulative-voting arithmetic.

questions.stem: A company elects 4 directors and 10,000,000 shares are voted. A shareholder owns 2,500,000 shares. Under cumulative voting, the maximum number of directors this shareholder can be sure to elect is closest to:
questions.explanation: Under cumulative voting, seats guaranteed require k × 10,000,000/5 + 1 shares. One seat needs 2,000,001 shares and two seats need 4,000,001, so 2.5 million shares guarantee 1 seat. Zero is the outcome under statutory voting, where the majority wins every seat; 2 would need over 4 million shares.

questions.stem: A founder holds Class B shares with 10 votes each, while public investors hold Class A shares with 1 vote each. This structure most likely:
options: lets the founder control the company with a minority of the equity
gives Class A holders pre-emptive rights not available to Class B
aligns voting power with economic ownership
questions.explanation: Multiple-vote shares separate control from cash-flow ownership, so a founder can control votes while owning a minority of the equity. That is the opposite of aligning votes with ownership. Pre-emptive rights are an economic right unrelated to the vote multiplier.

questions.stem: A pre-emptive right is best described as a shareholder's right to:
options: vote on all mergers and acquisitions
buy newly issued shares in proportion to existing holdings before they are offered to others
receive dividends before any other class of shareholder
questions.explanation: Pre-emptive rights protect existing holders from dilution by letting them buy new shares pro rata first. Voting on mergers is a voting right; dividend priority describes preferred shares.

questions.stem: In a market where most listed companies have a controlling family shareholder, the main governance conflict is most likely between:
options: bondholders and preferred shareholders
managers and dispersed shareholders
controlling shareholders and minority shareholders
questions.explanation: When ownership is concentrated, the controlling holder can extract private benefits at the expense of minority holders. The manager vs dispersed shareholder conflict dominates in widely held markets such as the US and UK.

questions.stem: A firm that researches company resolutions and issues voting recommendations to institutional investors is best described as a(n):
options: proxy advisor
asset owner
transfer agent
questions.explanation: Proxy advisors such as ISS and Glass Lewis analyse resolutions and recommend how to vote. Asset owners (e.g., pension funds) own the votes. A transfer agent keeps the share register but does not give voting advice.

questions.stem: A pension fund lends its shares through a securities lending programme. To vote at the upcoming annual meeting, the fund most likely needs to:
options: do nothing, because lent shares keep their votes with the lender
recall the shares before the record date
ask the proxy advisor to vote on its behalf
questions.explanation: Lent shares transfer the vote to the borrower. The lender must recall the shares before the record date to be on the register and vote. A proxy advisor cannot vote shares the fund does not hold on the record date.

questions.stem: Which party typically casts the votes for shares held in a mutual fund?
options: The company's board of directors
The individual investors in the fund, by default
The asset manager, on behalf of the fund's investors
questions.explanation: Asset managers usually vote the shares they manage, following their voting policy. Individual investors vote only if the manager offers pass-through voting. The investee company's board recommends but does not cast shareholders' votes.

questions.stem: 8,000,000 shares will be voted to elect 3 directors under cumulative voting. The minimum number of shares a minority group needs to guarantee electing 1 director is closest to:
questions.explanation: Shares needed = k × S/(N + 1) + 1 = 1 × 8,000,000/4 + 1 = 2,000,001. Using N instead of N + 1 gives 8,000,000/3 + 1 ≈ 2,666,668. Using k = 2 gives 4,000,001, which guarantees two seats.

questions.stem: Compared with statutory voting, cumulative voting most likely:
options: gives each share one vote per resolution regardless of seats
increases the ability of minority shareholders to obtain board representation
lets the majority shareholder win every board seat
questions.explanation: Cumulative voting multiplies votes by the number of seats and lets holders concentrate them, so minorities can win seats. Under statutory voting, each share gets one vote per seat and the majority wins every seat.

questions.stem: A shareholder resolution on executive pay passes, but the company is not legally required to act on it. The vote is best described as:
options: a proxy contest
binding
advisory
questions.explanation: Say-on-pay votes are advisory in many jurisdictions: they signal shareholder views but do not bind the board. Director elections and mergers are typically binding. A proxy contest is a fight over board seats.

questions.stem: An index provider excludes or underweights companies whose publicly traded shares carry little or no voting power. This policy most likely reflects concern that such structures:
options: weaken the accountability of controlling holders to outside shareholders
increase the company's dividend payout
reduce trading liquidity
questions.explanation: Low-vote public shares leave outside investors with economic exposure but little control, raising entrenchment and accountability concerns. Liquidity and payout are not the main governance objections to dual-class structures.

flashcards.back: Economic: dividends, residual claim, pre-emptive rights. Voting: elect directors, approve mergers, auditors, charter changes, (often advisory) pay.

flashcards.front: Cumulative voting: shares to guarantee k seats
flashcards.back: k × S/(N + 1) + 1, where S = shares voted and N = seats being elected.
One vote per share per seat → a majority holder wins every seat.
Pros: founder vision, deters hostile bids. Cons: entrenchment, weaker accountability, possible valuation discount.
Management: proposals. Board: recommends, oversees. Proxy advisor: research and recommendations. Asset manager: casts votes. Asset owner: owns votes, sets policy.
The vote goes with the lent share. Recall before the record date to vote.
Extra (e.g., double) votes for shareholders who hold for a minimum period; common in parts of continental Europe.

modules.title: Equity Issuance and Trading
modules.summary: How shares are first sold (IPOs, follow-ons, rights issues, private placements) and then traded (exchanges, dark pools, OTC), how to measure liquidity with spread, float, ADV and turnover, and the main types of equity index.

acca.note: FM covered IPOs, placings and rights issues as sources of finance. New for CFA: market microstructure (lit vs dark venues, order- vs quote-driven), the liquidity measures float, ADV, turnover and days-to-trade, and index types.

lessons.title: Primary markets: issuing shares

cards.title: Primary vs secondary
cards.body:
**Primary market**: the issuer sells new shares and receives the cash.
**Secondary market**: investors trade existing shares with each other; the company receives nothing.

A healthy secondary market makes primary issuance cheaper: investors pay more for shares they know they can sell.

cards.title: Ways to issue equity
rows: Investment bank buys the issue at a set price (firm commitment) and resells; prices via book-building
Bank sells as agent; issuer bears the risk of unsold shares
Existing shares list without new capital or underwriting
Listed shell raises cash, then merges with a private target
Existing holders get rights to buy new shares pro rata, usually at a discount
Sold to a few qualified investors; less disclosure, lower liquidity

cards.title: IPO pricing and underpricing
cards.body:
In **book-building**, the underwriter gathers investor orders to set the price. IPOs are on average **underpriced**: the first-day close is usually above the offer price. Underwriters benefit (easy sale, happy clients); the issuer "leaves money on the table".

A firm-commitment underwriter is exposed if the issue is overpriced and must sell below the offer price.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM framed rights issues around the **TERP** and the issuer's financing choice. CFA adds the investor angle: rights avoid dilution of **control** as well as value; underwriting types shift risk; and a rights issue at a discount is not a gift, because the share price adjusts to the TERP.

lessons.title: Trading venues and liquidity: float and ADV

cards.title: Where shares trade
rows: Order-driven: buy and sell orders matched by rules (price, then time priority)
Off-exchange; orders hidden; often matched at the exchange midpoint
Quote-driven: dealers post bid and ask and trade from inventory
Broker finds a counterparty for large or unusual blocks

cards.title: Why dark pools exist
cards.body:
Large institutions want to trade blocks without revealing their intention, which would move the price against them (**market impact**). Dark pools hide orders until execution.

The cost: less pre-trade transparency for the market as a whole, which can weaken price discovery on lit exchanges if too much volume moves off-exchange.

cards.title: Liquidity measures
cards.formula:
Float = shares outstanding − closely held/restricted shares
ADV = Σ daily volume ÷ number of days
Turnover = volume over period ÷ float
Days to trade = position ÷ (participation rate × ADV)
Relative spread = (ask − bid) ÷ midpoint
where: founders, insiders, governments, strategic holders, locked-up shares
share of daily volume you can trade without moving the price

cards.title: Float and ADV
cards.body:
500M shares outstanding. Founders hold 120M, a government 30M, restricted employee stock 10M. Index funds hold 40M.

Float = 500 − 120 − 30 − 10 = **340M** (68%). Index funds are ordinary investors, so their shares stay in the float.

Daily volumes (M): 2.1, 1.8, 2.4, 1.6, 2.6 → ADV = 10.5 ÷ 5 = **2.1M**.
Selling 3.15M shares at 20% participation takes 3.15 ÷ (0.20 × 2.1) = **7.5 days**.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body:
Do not subtract institutional or index-fund holdings from float: they can sell. Exclude only holders unlikely to trade (founders, insiders, governments, cross-holdings, locked-up shares).

Also, a high share count does not mean liquidity: a mega-cap with 10% float can be harder to trade than a smaller company with full float.

lessons.title: Types of equity indexes

cards.title: What an index is for
cards.body: An equity index tracks the value of a defined group of shares. Uses: **benchmark** for active managers, basis for **index funds and ETFs**, measure of market return, input to **beta** estimation, and model portfolio for asset allocation.

cards.title: Index types
rows: Most of a country's investable shares
Value vs growth (P/B, P/E, growth rates)

cards.title: Float-adjusted weight
cards.body:
Stock A: price 40, 100M shares, 60% float. Stock B: price 20, 300M shares, full float.

Float caps: A = 40 × 100 × 0.6 = 2,400M; B = 20 × 300 = 6,000M.
Weight of A = 2,400 ÷ 8,400 = **28.6%** (vs 40% on full market cap: 4,000 ÷ 10,000).

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Know **price return** vs **total return** indexes: a total return index reinvests dividends, so it grows faster. Index weighting and return arithmetic are tested mainly in Quant (Benchmarking Returns); here focus on index types and why float adjustment matters.

questions.stem: In which of the following does the issuing company receive the proceeds?
options: A secondary-market trade on an exchange
A seasoned (follow-on) offering of new shares
A block trade in a dark pool
questions.explanation: A follow-on offering of new shares is a primary-market transaction, so the cash goes to the issuer. Exchange trades and dark-pool block trades are secondary-market transfers between investors.

questions.stem: In a best-efforts offering, the risk that shares remain unsold is borne mainly by the:
options: investors who placed orders
underwriter
issuer
questions.explanation: In a best-efforts deal the bank acts only as agent, so unsold shares are the issuer's problem. In a firm-commitment underwriting the bank buys the issue and bears that risk.

questions.stem: A company lists its existing shares on an exchange without raising new capital and without an underwriter. This is a:
options: direct listing
SPAC merger
rights offering
questions.explanation: A direct listing makes existing shares tradable without a new issue or underwriting. A SPAC merger brings a private company public via a listed shell; a rights offering raises new capital from existing holders.

questions.stem: IPO underpricing is best evidenced by:
options: the offer price being above the first-day closing price on average
the first-day closing price being above the offer price on average
underwriters charging lower fees for larger issues
questions.explanation: Underpricing means the offer price is set below what the market pays on day one, so first-day returns are positive on average. The reverse would be overpricing; fee schedules are irrelevant.

questions.stem: A company has 800 million shares outstanding. The founding family holds 200 million, a sovereign fund with a strategic stake holds 80 million, and passive index funds hold 120 million. The float is closest to:
options: 600 million
400 million
520 million
questions.explanation: Float excludes closely held strategic stakes: 800 − 200 − 80 = 520 million. Index funds can trade, so their 120 million stays in the float. Subtracting them as well gives 400 million; subtracting only the family gives 600 million.

questions.stem: A stock's daily volumes over five days were 2.1, 1.8, 2.4, 1.6 and 2.6 million shares. A fund wants to sell 3.15 million shares while staying at no more than 20% of ADV each day. The number of trading days needed is closest to:
questions.explanation: ADV = (2.1 + 1.8 + 2.4 + 1.6 + 2.6)/5 = 2.1 million. Daily capacity = 0.20 × 2.1 = 0.42 million, so days = 3.15/0.42 = 7.5. Dividing by ADV without the participation cap gives 1.5; 10.5 is the five-day total volume.

questions.stem: A trading venue in which orders are not displayed before execution and trades are often matched at the exchange midpoint is best described as a(n):
options: quote-driven dealer market
dark pool
order-driven lit exchange
questions.explanation: Dark pools offer no pre-trade transparency and often cross orders at the lit-market midpoint, which helps institutions limit market impact. Dealer markets show dealer quotes; lit exchanges display the order book.

questions.stem: A stock has a bid of 49.90 and an ask of 50.10. Its relative (percentage) bid–ask spread is closest to:
questions.explanation: Relative spread = (50.10 − 49.90)/midpoint 50.00 = 0.20/50 = 0.40%. 0.20% is the half-spread; 0.80% doubles the spread.

questions.stem: Stock A: price 40, 100 million shares, 60% float. Stock B: price 20, 300 million shares, 100% float. In a float-adjusted market-cap index of these two stocks, the weight of A is closest to:
questions.explanation: Float caps: A = 40 × 100 × 0.6 = 2,400; B = 20 × 300 = 6,000. Weight A = 2,400/8,400 = 28.6%. Ignoring float gives 4,000/10,000 = 40%. A price weighting gives 40/60 = 66.7%.

questions.stem: An index that weights constituents by their sales or earnings rather than market capitalization is a(n):
options: price-weighted index
fundamentally weighted index
equal-weighted index
questions.explanation: Fundamental weighting uses company measures such as sales, earnings, book value or dividends; it tends to have a value tilt. Equal weighting uses 1/N; price weighting uses share prices.

questions.stem: Compared with a price return index on the same constituents, a total return index will most likely:
options: be identical, because dividends are reflected in prices
show a lower cumulative return
show a higher cumulative return if constituents pay dividends
questions.explanation: A total return index reinvests dividends, so over time it outgrows the price return index. Share prices drop on ex-dividend dates, so the price return index alone misses the income.

questions.stem: A stock has 340 million shares in its float and an ADV of 2.1 million shares. Assuming 250 trading days, annual turnover relative to float is closest to:
questions.explanation: Annual volume ≈ 2.1 × 250 = 525 million; turnover = 525/340 = 154%. 0.6% is one day's volume over float (2.1/340), not annualized. 162% wrongly uses 262 trading days (2.1 × 262/340).

questions.stem: Which holder's shares is most likely to be excluded when calculating a company's free float?
options: A pension fund holding 4% of the shares
The chief executive holding 12% of the shares
An ETF holding 3% of the shares
questions.explanation: Insider holdings such as a CEO's stake are treated as closely held and excluded from float. Pension funds and ETFs are investors that can trade, so their holdings remain in the float.

questions.stem: An institution wants to sell a very large block of shares while minimizing market impact. The venue it is most likely to use is a:
options: lit exchange using a market order
rights offering
dark pool
questions.explanation: Dark pools hide the order before execution, reducing information leakage and market impact for large blocks. A market order on a lit exchange exposes the order and can move the price. A rights offering is a primary-market issue by the company.

questions.stem: Compared with a market-cap-weighted index, an equal-weighted index of the same stocks most likely has:
options: a bias toward smaller companies and more frequent rebalancing
identical sector exposures
a bias toward large companies and lower turnover
questions.explanation: Equal weighting gives small companies the same weight as large ones, creating a small-cap tilt, and needs regular rebalancing as prices drift. Cap weighting self-rebalances and tilts to large companies.

questions.stem: A company's shares are 95% held by its founder and government, with 5% float. Compared with a peer of similar market capitalization and 100% float, the company's shares will most likely:
options: receive a higher weight in a float-adjusted index
have lower ADV and be harder for large investors to trade
have higher turnover relative to shares outstanding
questions.explanation: With only 5% of shares available to trade, volumes and ADV tend to be low, so large positions take longer to build or exit. Float adjustment cuts its index weight, and turnover relative to shares outstanding will be low.

flashcards.back: Shares outstanding − closely held/restricted shares (insiders, founders, governments, strategic cross-holdings, locked-up shares).
Average daily volume = Σ daily volume ÷ number of days.
Position ÷ (participation rate × ADV).
Trading volume over a period ÷ float (or shares outstanding).
Off-exchange venue with no pre-trade transparency; used to trade blocks with less market impact.
Order-driven: buyers' and sellers' orders matched by rules (exchanges). Quote-driven: dealers post bid/ask and trade from inventory (OTC).
Firm commitment: underwriter buys the issue and bears unsold risk. Best efforts: underwriter acts as agent; issuer bears unsold risk.
Total return index reinvests dividends; price return index ignores them.

modules.title: Sources of Equity Returns
modules.summary: Equity investors earn returns from dividends and price changes. Covers cash and stock dividends, splits, reverse splits and repurchases, the dividend timeline, and price vs total return.

acca.note: FM covered dividend policy, scrip dividends and share buybacks from the company's side. New for CFA: the payment chronology (ex-date vs record date), the mechanical effect of splits and stock dividends, buyback effects on EPS and BVPS, and price vs total return.

lessons.title: Dividends and the payment timeline

cards.title: Types of cash distribution
cards.body:
- **Regular cash dividend**: paid on a set schedule (quarterly in the US, semi-annual in much of Europe and Asia).
- **Special (extra) dividend**: one-off, e.g., after an unusually good year or asset sale.
- **Liquidating dividend**: a return of capital, e.g., when winding down or selling a division.

Companies are reluctant to cut regular dividends because markets read a cut as a negative signal about future earnings.

cards.title: Dividend chronology
rows: Board announces amount, record and payment dates
First day the share trades without the dividend; price drops by ≈ the dividend
Shareholders on the register this day receive the dividend

cards.title: Ex-date vs record date
cards.body:
To be on the register by the record date, you must buy before the trade settles. So the ex-date depends on the settlement cycle:
- **T+2**: ex-date is one business day before the record date.
- **T+1** (US since 2024): ex-date and record date are the same day.

Buy **before** the ex-date → you get the dividend. Buy **on or after** it → the seller gets it.

cards.title: Ex-dividend price drop
cards.body:
A share closes at 50.00 the day before its ex-date. The dividend is 1.00.

All else equal it should open near **49.00** on the ex-date: buyers no longer get the 1.00, so they pay 1.00 less. A holder is no richer or poorer: 49 in shares + 1 in cash = 50.

In practice, taxes on dividends can make the drop slightly smaller than the dividend.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: The ex-date is the date that matters to traders. If asked "who receives the dividend", find the trade date and compare it with the ex-date, not the record date.

lessons.title: Stock dividends, splits and repurchases

cards.title: Stock dividends and splits
cards.body:
Both issue more shares to holders **pro rata**: ownership and total value are unchanged; the price falls in proportion.

- **Stock dividend** 10%: 200 shares at 33 → 220 shares at 30.
- **Stock split** 3-for-2: 1,000 shares at 60 → 1,500 at 40.
- **Reverse split** 1-for-5: 50,000 shares at 2 → 10,000 at 10.

Splits make shares look affordable; reverse splits lift a low price (e.g., to meet listing rules). A stock dividend moves retained earnings to paid-in capital; total equity is unchanged.

cards.title: Share repurchase methods
rows: Buy gradually on the exchange; most common and most flexible
Offer to buy a set number of shares at a fixed premium price
Holders bid prices within a range; company pays the lowest price that fills the target
Buy a block from a large holder (sometimes at a premium)

cards.title: Buyback effect on EPS
cards.body:
Net income 10M, 5M shares, EPS 2.00, price 40. The company borrows 20M at an after-tax cost of 4% and buys 0.5M shares.

New earnings = 10 − 0.04 × 20 = 9.2M; new shares = 4.5M.
EPS = 9.2 ÷ 4.5 = **2.04** (up).

Rule: EPS rises if the **earnings yield** (E/P = 2/40 = 5%) exceeds the after-tax cost of funds (4%).

cards.title: Buyback effect on BVPS
cards.body:
Book equity 100M, 10M shares (BVPS 10). The company uses cash to buy back 1M shares at 15.

New equity = 100 − 15 = 85M; shares = 9M.
BVPS = 85 ÷ 9 = **9.44** (down).

Rule: BVPS falls when the buyback price exceeds BVPS (P/B > 1), and rises when shares are bought below book.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM argued (Miller–Modigliani) that dividend policy is irrelevant in perfect markets. CFA cares about the **mechanics**: a buyback is economically like a cash dividend paid only to sellers, and it changes EPS and BVPS. A higher EPS after a buyback does not by itself create value.

lessons.title: Price return and total return

cards.title: Holding-period returns
One- and two-year total return
cards.body:
Buy at 40. Year 1: dividend 1.00, price 42. Year 2: dividend 1.20, price 45.

Year 1 TR = (42 − 40 + 1) ÷ 40 = **7.5%**
Year 2 TR = (45 − 42 + 1.2) ÷ 42 = **10.0%**
Two-year TR = 1.075 × 1.10 − 1 = **18.25%**

Two-year price return alone = (45 − 40) ÷ 40 = 12.5%.

cards.title: Where total return comes from
cards.body:
Over long periods, dividends and their reinvestment account for a large share of equity total return, especially in mature, high-payout markets.

A useful split: total return ≈ dividend yield + growth in earnings per share + change in valuation multiple (P/E). Multiple changes dominate short-run returns; dividends and earnings growth dominate long-run returns.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Adjust for splits before computing returns: if a 2-for-1 split happens during the year, compare the end price with **half** the starting price (or double the end price). Also, chain-link multi-period returns; do not add them.

questions.stem: The first day on which a buyer of a share is no longer entitled to the declared dividend is the:
options: payment date
declaration date
ex-dividend date
questions.explanation: From the ex-dividend date the share trades without the dividend, so new buyers do not receive it. The declaration date announces the dividend; the payment date is when cash is paid.

questions.stem: A share closes at 50.00 the day before going ex-dividend. The dividend is 1.00. Ignoring taxes and new information, the share's opening price on the ex-date is closest to:
questions.explanation: The price should fall by about the dividend, because buyers from the ex-date no longer receive it: 50.00 − 1.00 = 49.00. Holders are no worse off because they keep the 1.00 cash.

questions.stem: In a market with T+1 settlement, the ex-dividend date is most likely:
options: two business days before the record date
the same day as the record date
the same day as the payment date
questions.explanation: Under T+1, a trade on the record date settles the next day, too late to be on the register, while a trade the day before settles on the record date. So the ex-date coincides with the record date. Under T+2 it would be one business day before the record date.

questions.stem: An investor owns 1,000 shares priced at 60. The company executes a 3-for-2 stock split. Immediately after the split, the investor most likely holds:
options: 1,500 shares priced at 60
667 shares priced at 90
1,500 shares priced at 40
questions.explanation: A 3-for-2 split gives 3 new shares for every 2: 1,000 × 1.5 = 1,500 shares. Total value is unchanged at 60,000, so price = 60,000/1,500 = 40. 667 shares at 90 is a 2-for-3 reverse split.

questions.stem: A company has net income of 10 million, 5 million shares and a share price of 40. It borrows 20 million at an after-tax cost of 4% and buys back shares at 40. EPS after the buyback is closest to:
questions.explanation: Shares bought = 20/40 = 0.5 million, leaving 4.5 million. Earnings = 10 − 0.04 × 20 = 9.2 million. EPS = 9.2/4.5 = 2.04. 2.00 is the original EPS; 2.22 ignores the interest cost (10/4.5).

questions.stem: A company with book equity of 100 million and 10 million shares uses cash to repurchase 1 million shares at 15. Book value per share after the buyback is closest to:
questions.explanation: New equity = 100 − 15 = 85 million; shares = 9 million; BVPS = 85/9 = 9.44. BVPS falls because the shares were bought above book value (15 > 10). 10.00 is the original BVPS; 11.11 forgets to reduce equity by the cash paid (100/9).

questions.stem: In a Dutch auction tender offer, the company:
options: negotiates a single block purchase with a major holder
buys shares gradually on the open market
pays the lowest price within a range that allows it to buy the target number of shares
questions.explanation: In a Dutch auction, holders tender at prices within a stated range and the company pays the lowest clearing price that fills its target, the same price for everyone. Open-market purchases and direct negotiation are separate methods.

questions.stem: A share is bought at 40, pays a dividend of 1.00 and is sold one year later at 42. The total return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Total return = (42 − 40 + 1)/40 = 3/40 = 7.5%. Price return alone is 2/40 = 5.0%; 2.5% is the dividend yield only.

questions.stem: A share bought at 40 pays 1.00 and ends year 1 at 42, then pays 1.20 and ends year 2 at 45. The two-year holding-period total return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Year 1 = (42 − 40 + 1)/40 = 7.5%. Year 2 = (45 − 42 + 1.2)/42 = 10.0%. Compounded: 1.075 × 1.10 − 1 = 18.25%. Adding the two returns gives 17.5%; 12.5% is the two-year price return only.

questions.stem: An investor holds 200 shares priced at 33. The company pays a 10% stock dividend. Assuming no other change, the investor's position is most likely:
options: 220 shares at 33.00, worth 7,260
200 shares at 30.00, worth 6,000
220 shares at 30.00, worth 6,600
questions.explanation: A 10% stock dividend gives 20 extra shares (220 total). Total value is unchanged at 200 × 33 = 6,600, so price = 6,600/220 = 30.00. A stock dividend does not create value, so 7,260 is wrong; 6,000 forgets the new shares.

questions.stem: A debt-funded buyback will most likely increase EPS when:
options: the company's earnings yield exceeds the after-tax cost of the funds used
the share price is below book value per share
the after-tax cost of debt exceeds the earnings yield
questions.explanation: Each share retired removes its share of earnings (the earnings yield) while the funding costs the after-tax rate. If E/P > after-tax cost, EPS rises. Price vs book value determines the BVPS effect, not the EPS effect.

questions.stem: A company with 50,000 shares trading at 2.00 completes a 1-for-5 reverse split. An investor who owned 2% of the company before the split most likely owns afterwards:
options: 2% of 250,000 shares priced at 0.40
2% of 10,000 shares priced at 10.00
10% of 10,000 shares priced at 10.00
questions.explanation: A 1-for-5 reverse split combines every 5 shares into 1: 50,000/5 = 10,000 shares, and the price rises fivefold to 10.00. Ownership percentages are unchanged at 2%. 250,000 at 0.40 is a 5-for-1 forward split.

questions.stem: A company pays its usual quarterly dividend and also a one-off payment after selling a division. The one-off payment is best described as a:
options: stock dividend
regular dividend
special dividend
questions.explanation: A one-off cash payment on top of the regular dividend, often after an asset sale or exceptional year, is a special (extra) dividend. A stock dividend is paid in shares, not cash.

questions.stem: Investor A buys a share the day before the ex-dividend date; Investor B buys the same share on the ex-dividend date. Which investor receives the dividend?
options: Investor A only
Investor B only
Both investors
questions.explanation: Buying before the ex-date means the trade settles in time to be on the register at the record date, so A receives the dividend. B buys on the ex-date, so the dividend stays with the seller. Only one holder can receive each dividend.

flashcards.back: Declaration → ex-dividend → holder-of-record → payment.
T+1: ex-date = record date. T+2: ex-date is one business day before record date.

flashcards.front: Effect of a stock split or stock dividend
flashcards.back: More shares, proportionally lower price; total value and ownership % unchanged.
EPS rises if earnings yield (E/P) > after-tax cost of funds used; falls if lower.
BVPS falls if shares are bought above BVPS (P/B > 1); rises if bought below.
(P_{1} − P_{0} + D) ÷ P_{0}; multi-period returns are chain-linked: Π(1 + R_{t}) − 1.
Holders bid within a price range; the company pays the lowest price that fills its target to all accepted tenders.

modules.title: Introduction to Equity Valuation
modules.summary: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. Covers intrinsic value vs market price, book value vs market cap vs enterprise value as value indicators, and the three families of valuation models with their pros and cons.

acca.note: FM business valuation covered asset-based, earnings (P/E) and dividend/cash-flow methods. New for CFA: EV as the firm-level value measure, the framing of over/undervaluation against intrinsic value, and a structured pros and cons comparison of model families.

lessons.title: Price vs value; book value, market cap and EV

cards.title: Intrinsic value vs price
cards.body:
**Intrinsic value** is the analyst's estimate of what a share is worth given its expected cash flows and risk. **Market price** is what it trades at.

- Value > price → **undervalued** → buy
- Value < price → **overvalued** → sell or short
- Value ≈ price → **fairly valued**

A gap only matters if it is large relative to the uncertainty in your estimate and you expect the market to close it.

cards.title: Three "size" measures
rows: Market value of equity = price × shares
Ignores debt; it is the price, not an independent value
Value of the operating business to all capital providers
Needs market values of debt and other claims

cards.title: Enterprise value
cards.formula: EV = market cap + MV of debt + preferred + non-controlling interest − cash and short-term investments
cards.note: Cash is subtracted because a buyer of the whole firm effectively gets it back.

cards.title: EV example
cards.body:
50M shares at 30 → market cap 1,500. Debt 600, preferred 100, NCI 50, cash 250.

EV = 1,500 + 600 + 100 + 50 − 250 = **2,000**.
With EBITDA of 250, EV/EBITDA = **8.0×**.

If your DCF says intrinsic share value is 45 vs a price of 40, the share looks undervalued by (45 − 40) ÷ 40 = 12.5%.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Use EV (not market cap) with pre-interest measures such as EBITDA, EBIT or sales, because those flows belong to all capital providers. Use market cap (price) with post-interest measures such as net income or book equity.

lessons.title: Families of valuation models

cards.title: Model categories
rows: Discounting expected future cash flows or returns
Comparing a multiple with peers or a justified level
Adjusted net asset value, liquidation value

cards.title: Pros and cons
rows: Grounded in fundamentals; forces explicit assumptions
Very sensitive to growth and discount rate; terminal value dominates
Peers may all be mispriced; hard to find true comparables
Good for asset-heavy, financial or failing firms
Ignores going-concern earning power and intangibles

cards.title: Choosing a model
cards.body:
- Stable payer, minority stake → **DDM**
- Non-payer or control perspective → **FCFE/FCFF**
- Negative or volatile FCF but meaningful book value (e.g., banks) → **residual income**
- Many good peers → **multiples** (as a cross-check at least)
- Resource firms, holding companies, liquidation → **asset-based**

Analysts usually triangulate: DCF as anchor, multiples as a sanity check.

cards.title: Going-concern vs liquidation value
cards.body: **Going-concern value** assumes the firm keeps operating. **Liquidation value** is what the assets fetch if sold and the firm closes. For a healthy firm, going-concern value is higher; if liquidation value exceeds going-concern value, the owners would be better off selling the assets.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM grouped methods as asset-based, income/earnings-based and cash-flow-based, mostly for unlisted company acquisitions. CFA uses the same idea but frames the output as **intrinsic value vs market price** for a listed share, and expects you to match the model to the company's characteristics.

questions.stem: A company has 50 million shares priced at 30, debt (market value) of 600 million, preferred stock of 100 million, non-controlling interest of 50 million and cash of 250 million. Its enterprise value is closest to:
options: 1,500 million
2,000 million
2,500 million
questions.explanation: EV = 1,500 + 600 + 100 + 50 − 250 = 2,000 million. 1,500 million is market cap only; 2,500 million adds cash instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem: An analyst estimates a share's intrinsic value at 45. It trades at 40. The share is best described as:
options: undervalued by 11.1%
overvalued by 12.5%
undervalued by 12.5%
questions.explanation: Value exceeds price, so the share is undervalued. Measured against price: (45 − 40)/40 = 12.5%. Measuring against value gives 5/45 = 11.1%, which is the percentage the price could fall short of value, not the usual upside measure.

questions.stem: Which multiple is most internally consistent?
options: EV ÷ EBITDA
EV ÷ net income
Market cap ÷ EBITDA
questions.explanation: EBITDA is a pre-interest flow to all capital providers, so it pairs with EV. Market cap pairs with post-interest measures such as net income; EV/net income and market cap/EBITDA mix claims.

questions.stem: Book value of equity is likely to be a poor indicator of intrinsic value for a company whose main assets are:
options: cash and marketable securities
internally developed brands and software
loans carried at amortized cost close to fair value
questions.explanation: Internally generated intangibles are mostly expensed, not capitalized, so book value understates their worth. Cash, securities and loans near fair value are reflected reasonably well in book value.

questions.stem: A residual income model belongs to which family of valuation models?
options: Multiplier models
Asset-based models
Present value models
questions.explanation: Residual income values a firm as book value plus the present value of future earnings above the required return, so it is a present value model. Multipliers compare ratios; asset-based models value net assets directly.

questions.stem: An analyst values an oil exploration company with large proven reserves and volatile cash flows. The approach most likely to be useful is a(n):
options: asset-based valuation
P/E multiple based on current earnings
dividend discount model
questions.explanation: For natural resource firms, the market value of reserves drives value, so an asset-based approach fits. Dividends and earnings are volatile and may say little about long-term value.

questions.stem: A key limitation of the method of comparables is that:
options: it requires a forecast of cash flows to infinity
the whole peer group may be mispriced
it cannot be applied to companies with positive earnings
questions.explanation: Comparables give relative value: if peers are overvalued, the target looks cheap even if it is not. DCF models need long-term cash flow forecasts; multiples work best with positive earnings.

questions.stem: Firm A and Firm B have identical EBITDA and identical market capitalizations. Firm A has no debt and large cash balances; Firm B is highly levered. Compared with Firm B, Firm A will most likely have:
options: a higher EV/EBITDA
the same EV/EBITDA
a lower EV/EBITDA
questions.explanation: EV = market cap + debt − cash. With equal market caps, Firm A's EV is lower (no debt, cash subtracted) and Firm B's is higher (debt added). With equal EBITDA, A has the lower EV/EBITDA.

questions.stem: A company's enterprise value is 2,000 million. It has debt of 600 million, preferred stock of 100 million, non-controlling interest of 50 million and cash of 250 million. The market value of its common equity is closest to:
options: 1,500 million
2,000 million
1,250 million
questions.explanation: Equity = EV − debt − preferred − NCI + cash = 2,000 − 600 − 100 − 50 + 250 = 1,500 million. 1,250 million forgets to add back cash; 2,000 million is EV itself.

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly favours a free cash flow model over a dividend discount model?
options: A utility with a stable payout tied to earnings
A growing company that pays no dividends and is a takeover target
A mature bank with a long dividend history
questions.explanation: When a company pays no dividends, or the investor takes a control perspective (takeover), dividends do not reflect value creation, so FCF models fit. Stable, earnings-linked payers suit the DDM.

questions.stem: A company's estimated liquidation value exceeds its going-concern value. This most likely indicates that:
options: the share is fairly valued at book value
the company should keep operating to maximize value
shareholders would be better off if the assets were sold
questions.explanation: If assets are worth more sold than used in the business, continuing destroys value, so selling (liquidating) would benefit owners. Book value is unrelated to that comparison.

flashcards.back: Undervalued: intrinsic value > price. Overvalued: intrinsic value < price.
Market cap + MV debt + preferred + NCI − cash and short-term investments.

flashcards.front: Which multiples pair with EV vs price?
flashcards.back: EV: pre-interest flows (EBITDA, EBIT, sales). Price/market cap: post-interest (net income, book equity).
Present value (DDM, FCFE, FCFF, RI); multiplier (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA); asset-based (adjusted NAV, liquidation).
Highly sensitive to discount rate, growth and terminal value assumptions.
Relative only: if the peer group is mispriced, so is the estimate.
Going concern: firm keeps operating. Liquidation: assets sold piecemeal. Healthy firms: going concern > liquidation.

modules.title: Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) and Growth Models
modules.summary: The core present-value toolkit: Gordon growth and multistage dividend discount models, preferred stock valuation and contingency features, FCFF and FCFE models, and the residual income model, plus the pitfalls of growth assumptions.

acca.note: FM covered the dividend valuation model (Gordon growth), g = b × r and K_{e} = D_{1}/P_{0} + g; AFM covered free cash flow valuation. New for CFA: multistage DDM timing, the precise FCFF/FCFE definitions, residual income, and preferred contingency features.

lessons.title: Gordon growth model and preferred stock

cards.title: Gordon (constant) growth DDM
where: constant growth rate forever, g < r
cards.note: Implied required return: r = D_{1}/P_{0} + g (dividend yield + growth).

cards.title: Sustainable growth and preferred stock
cards.formula:
g = b × ROE = (1 − payout) × ROE
Perpetual preferred: V_{0} = D_{p} ÷ r_{p}
cards.note: Example: payout 40%, ROE 15% → g = 0.6 × 15% = 9%. Preferred 6% on 100 par, r_{p} = 7.5% → 6 ÷ 0.075 = 80.

cards.title: When GGM fits
cards.body:
Use it for mature, stable firms whose dividends grow roughly with the economy. Value is very sensitive to (r − g): with r = 9%, moving g from 5% to 6% raises value from 52.50 to 2.12 ÷ 0.03 ≈ 70.7.

If g ≥ r the formula breaks (value would be infinite or negative): long-run g must be below r and, realistically, near nominal GDP growth.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: Same model as FM's dividend valuation model, with the same "D_{1} not D_{0}" trap. CFA writes **r** for the cost of equity (FM: K_{e}) and **ROE** for the return on reinvested funds (FM: r). Also expect GGM to be used for the **terminal value** inside multistage models.

lessons.title: Multistage DDM, growth pitfalls and preferred features

cards.title: Multistage DDM
where: last year of the high-growth stage
cards.note: The terminal value V_{n} is a value at time n, so discount it n periods, not n + 1.

cards.title: Shortcomings of growth assumptions
cards.body:
- **Terminal value dominates**: often 60–80% of total value, so small changes in g_{L} or r swing the answer.
- **High growth cannot last**: competition erodes excess returns; fade growth toward GDP.
- **g must be consistent**: growth should be supported by reinvestment (g = b × ROE) and margins.
- **Abrupt drops** from high to stable growth are unrealistic; a three-stage model or linear fade helps.
- Using a g too close to r creates absurdly high values.

cards.title: Preferred shares with contingency features
cards.body:
- **Callable**: issuer can redeem at the call price. If rates fall, value is capped near the call price. Value = straight value − value of the call.
- **Putable/retractable**: holder can sell back at a set price → acts as a floor. Value = straight value + put.
- **Convertible**: holder can switch into common → value ≥ conversion value.
- **Fixed maturity**: value as a bond: PV of dividends + PV of redemption price.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Two classic multistage errors: (1) computing V_{n} with D_{n} instead of D_{n+1}; (2) discounting V_{n} for n + 1 periods. In the example these give 24.57 and 23.43 instead of 25.62.

lessons.title: FCFF, FCFE and residual income

cards.title: Free cash flows
cards.formula:
FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + Dep − FCInv − WCInv
FCFF = NI + NCC + Int(1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv
FCFE = FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing
FCFE = NI + NCC − FCInv − WCInv + net borrowing

cards.title: Single-stage FCF valuation
cards.formula:
V_{firm} = FCFF_{1} ÷ (WACC − g)
V_{equity} = V_{firm} − MV of debt
V_{equity} = FCFE_{1} ÷ (r − g)
cards.note: Match the cash flow to the rate: FCFF ↔ WACC; FCFE ↔ cost of equity.

cards.title: FCFF to share value
cards.body:
EBIT 500, tax 25%, depreciation 80, FCInv 120, WCInv 30.
FCFF = 500 × 0.75 + 80 − 120 − 30 = **305**

Interest 40, net borrowing 20:
FCFE = 305 − 40 × 0.75 + 20 = **295**

If next year's FCFF = 305, WACC 9%, g 4%: firm = 305 ÷ 0.05 = 6,100; less debt 1,500 = 4,600; ÷ 100M shares = **46.00**.

cards.title: Residual income (RI)
cards.note: Positive RI only when ROE > r: value is created above book.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: RI is useful when FCF is negative (heavy investment), dividends are absent, or for financial firms where book value is meaningful. Most of its value is recognised early (book value is up front), so it is less reliant on terminal value than DDM or FCF models.

questions.stem: A company just paid a dividend of 2.00. Dividends are expected to grow at 5% forever and the required return is 9%. The value of the share is closest to:
A perpetual preferred share has a par value of 100 and a 6% dividend. If the required return is 7.5%, its value is closest to:
questions.explanation: V = D/r = 6/0.075 = 80.00. 125.00 would be the value if the required return were 4.8%; 75.00 discounts at 8% (6/0.08) rather than 7.5%. Because r > coupon rate, the share trades below par.

questions.stem: A share trades at 40. Next year's dividend is expected to be 1.60 and dividends grow at 6% a year. The implied required return is closest to:
A company pays out 40% of earnings and earns an ROE of 15%. Its sustainable growth rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: g = b × ROE = (1 − 0.40) × 15% = 9.0%. 6.0% wrongly multiplies the payout ratio by ROE; 15.0% assumes full retention.

questions.stem: D_{0} = 1.00. Dividends grow at 20% for three years and then at 5% forever. The required return is 11%. The value of the share today is closest to:
Market interest rates fall significantly. Compared with an otherwise identical non-callable preferred share, a callable preferred share's value will most likely:
options: be unaffected
rise by more
rise by less, as it is capped near the call price
questions.explanation: Lower rates raise the value of fixed dividends, but the issuer will call the share once its value exceeds the call price, so the callable share's upside is capped. The call option belongs to the issuer, so it subtracts value from the holder.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant weakness of a two-stage DDM with an abrupt drop from high to stable growth?
options: Value is highly sensitive to the terminal growth rate, and the abrupt drop is often unrealistic
It discounts dividends at the risk-free rate
It cannot be used for companies that pay dividends
questions.explanation: The terminal value typically dominates, so small changes in long-run growth (or r) move the value a lot, and real firms fade gradually rather than dropping overnight. The model is designed for dividend payers and discounts at the required return on equity, not the risk-free rate.

questions.stem: EBIT is 500, the tax rate is 25%, depreciation is 80, fixed capital investment is 120 and working capital investment is 30. FCFF is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + Dep − FCInv − WCInv = 375 + 80 − 120 − 30 = 305. 225 forgets to add back depreciation (375 − 120 − 30); 335 ignores the working capital investment.

questions.stem: FCFF is 305, interest expense is 40, the tax rate is 25% and net borrowing is 20. FCFE is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFE = FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing = 305 − 30 + 20 = 295. 285 deducts the full pre-tax interest (305 − 40 + 20). 305 ignores payments to and from lenders.

questions.stem: Next year's FCFF is expected to be 305 million and to grow at 4% forever. WACC is 9%. Debt has a market value of 1,500 million and there are 100 million shares. The value per share is closest to:
questions.explanation: Firm value = 305/(0.09 − 0.04) = 6,100. Equity = 6,100 − 1,500 = 4,600; per share 46.00. 61.00 forgets to deduct debt. 63.44 grows the FCFF again (305 × 1.04/0.05) without deducting debt.

questions.stem: Book value per share at the start of the year is 20, expected EPS is 3.00 and the cost of equity is 10%. Expected residual income per share for the year is closest to:
questions.explanation: RI = E − r × B_{0} = 3.00 − 0.10 × 20 = 1.00. 2.00 is the equity charge; 3.00 ignores the cost of equity entirely.

questions.stem: A share has book value per share of 20, a constant ROE of 15%, a cost of equity of 10% and a constant growth rate of 5%. Using a single-stage residual income model, its value is closest to:
questions.explanation: V_{0} = B_{0} + (ROE − r) × B_{0}/(r − g) = 20 + 0.05 × 20/0.05 = 40. Consistent with GGM: payout = 1 − 5%/15% = 2/3, so D_{1} = 2 and 2/0.05 = 40. 30.00 treats RI as a no-growth perpetuity (20 + 1/0.10); 60.00 adds the full GGM value to book value (20 + 40), double counting.

questions.stem: A share trades at 50. The last dividend was 2.00 and the required return is 10%. The constant growth rate implied by the Gordon growth model is closest to:
Net income is 200, depreciation is 60, fixed capital investment is 90, working capital investment is 20 and net borrowing is 30. FCFE is closest to:
questions.explanation: FCFE = NI + NCC − FCInv − WCInv + net borrowing = 200 + 60 − 90 − 20 + 30 = 180. 150 ignores net borrowing; 120 subtracts borrowing instead of adding it.

questions.stem: B_{0} = 50 and the cost of equity is 10%. Expected EPS is 6.00 in year 1 and 7.00 in year 2; the year 1 dividend is 2.00. Residual income is assumed to be zero after year 2. Using clean-surplus accounting, the value per share is closest to:

Which valuation model is most appropriate for a company with negative free cash flow for the next several years because of heavy expansion, no dividends, but a reliable book value and positive expected ROE above its cost of equity?
options: Residual income model
FCFE model
Dividend discount model
questions.explanation: RI works with accounting data even when dividends are absent and FCF is negative; value is book value plus PV of returns above the cost of equity. A DDM needs dividends, and FCFE with years of negative flows pushes most value into an uncertain terminal value.

flashcards.back: g = b × ROE = (1 − payout) × ROE.
V_{n} = D_{n+1}/(r − g_{L}), discounted n periods (not n + 1).
EBIT(1 − t) + Dep − FCInv − WCInv; discount at WACC.
FCFF − Int(1 − t) + net borrowing; discount at cost of equity.
RI_{t} = E_{t} − r·B_{t−1}; V_{0} = B_{0} + Σ PV(RI). Positive only when ROE > r.

modules.title: Relative Value Equity Valuation Approaches
modules.summary: Valuing a share by comparing multiples: the method of comparables (peers) vs the method of forecasted fundamentals (justified multiples), price and EV multiples, trailing vs forward measures, and how to choose a peer group.

acca.note: FM covered the P/E (earnings) valuation method: value = P/E × earnings, adjusted for unlisted status. New for CFA: justified multiples derived from the DDM, P/B, P/S and EV multiples, trailing vs forward conventions, and disciplined peer-group selection.

lessons.title: The method of comparables with P/E

cards.title: Two ways to use a multiple
cards.body:
- **Method of comparables**: compare a firm's multiple with peers' (median or mean). Higher than peers with similar fundamentals → relatively **overvalued**. Based on the **law of one price**.
- **Method of forecasted fundamentals**: compare the actual multiple with a **justified** multiple derived from a DCF model (growth, risk, payout).

Comparables tell you relative value; fundamentals tell you intrinsic value.

cards.title: Trailing vs forward P/E
cards.formula:
Trailing P/E = P_{0} ÷ EPS over last 12 months
Forward (leading) P/E = P_{0} ÷ next 12 months' expected EPS
cards.note: For a growing firm, forward P/E < trailing P/E because expected EPS is higher.

cards.title: Valuing with peer P/E
cards.body:
Peer median forward P/E = 18. Target's forward EPS = 2.50.
Estimated value = 18 × 2.50 = **45.00**.

The target trades at 44, with trailing EPS 2.20:
Trailing P/E = 44 ÷ 2.20 = 20.0; forward P/E = 44 ÷ 2.50 = 17.6.

Compare like with like: forward with forward. On a forward basis (17.6 vs 18) the target looks slightly cheap.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: FM's P/E method is the method of comparables. CFA adds terminology (**trailing** = historical EPS, **forward/leading** = expected EPS) and insists the peer multiple and the target's EPS use the same basis. Also, a low P/E is only "cheap" if growth and risk are similar to peers.

lessons.title: Justified multiples, other multiples and peer selection

cards.title: Justified multiples (from GGM)
cards.formula:
Leading P/E = (1 − b) ÷ (r − g)
Trailing P/E = (1 − b)(1 + g) ÷ (r − g)
P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (r − g)
cards.note: P/E rises with payout and growth, falls with r. P/B > 1 only if ROE > r.

cards.title: Justified multiples example
cards.body:
Payout 40%, r = 10%, g = 6%:
Leading P/E = 0.40 ÷ 0.04 = **10.0**
Trailing P/E = 10.0 × 1.06 = **10.6**

ROE 14%, r 10%, g 6%:
P/B = (0.14 − 0.06) ÷ (0.10 − 0.06) = **2.0**

If the share trades at 15× forward earnings vs a justified 10×, it looks overvalued on fundamentals.

cards.title: Which multiple when
rows: Comparing firms with different leverage, capital-intensive firms

cards.title: Valuing with EV/EBITDA
cards.body:
Peer EV/EBITDA = 9×. Target EBITDA = 400, debt 1,200, cash 200, 100M shares.

EV = 9 × 400 = 3,600
Equity = 3,600 − 1,200 + 200 = 2,400
Per share = **24.00**

Traps: forgetting debt gives 36.00; subtracting cash gives 22.00.

cards.title: Choosing the peer group
cards.body:
Good comparables share the same **business mix, growth, risk, size and capital structure**, and the same accounting basis.

Steps: start with an industry classification (GICS/ICB), screen by size and region, then drop firms with different business models. Prefer the **median** multiple (outliers distort the mean). Adjust for differences: a firm with faster growth or lower risk deserves a higher multiple.

questions.stem: The method of comparables values a company by:
options: deriving a justified multiple from its growth, payout and required return
comparing its multiple with those of similar companies
discounting its expected free cash flows
questions.explanation: The method of comparables benchmarks a firm's multiple against peers (law of one price). Deriving a justified multiple from fundamentals is the forecasted fundamentals method; discounting cash flows is a DCF approach.

questions.stem: The peer-group median forward P/E is 18. The target's EPS was 2.20 over the last 12 months and is expected to be 2.50 over the next 12 months. Using the method of comparables, the target's estimated value is closest to:
questions.explanation: A forward multiple must be applied to forward EPS: value = 18 × 2.50 = 45.00. 39.60 applies the forward multiple to trailing EPS (18 × 2.20), a basis mismatch. 42.30 uses the average of trailing and forward EPS (18 × 2.35).

questions.stem: A share trades at 44. Its EPS over the last 12 months was 2.20 and its expected EPS for the next 12 months is 2.50. Its trailing and forward P/E ratios are closest to:
options: 20.0 trailing; 17.6 forward
20.0 trailing; 20.0 forward
17.6 trailing; 20.0 forward
questions.explanation: Trailing P/E = 44/2.20 = 20.0; forward P/E = 44/2.50 = 17.6. The forward P/E is lower because expected EPS is higher. 17.6 trailing and 20.0 forward swaps the two; 20.0 for both ignores the higher expected EPS.

questions.stem: A company pays out 40% of earnings, has a required return of 10% and a sustainable growth rate of 6%. Its justified leading P/E is closest to:
questions.explanation: Justified leading P/E = payout/(r − g) = 0.40/0.04 = 10.0. 10.6 is the justified trailing P/E (× 1.06). 6.7 divides the payout by g alone (0.40/0.06) instead of by r − g.

questions.stem: A bank has an ROE of 14%, a required return on equity of 10% and a sustainable growth rate of 6%. Its justified P/B ratio is closest to:
A target has EBITDA of 400 million, debt of 1,200 million, cash of 200 million and 100 million shares. Peers trade at 9× EV/EBITDA. The estimated value per share is closest to:
questions.explanation: EV = 9 × 400 = 3,600. Equity = 3,600 − 1,200 + 200 = 2,400; per share 24.00. 36.00 treats EV as equity value; 22.00 subtracts cash instead of adding it.

questions.stem: For a company currently reporting losses, the multiple most likely to be useful is:
options: P/E
P/S
PEG
questions.explanation: With negative earnings, P/E (and P/E-based PEG) is not meaningful, while sales are positive, so P/S still works (though it ignores margins).

questions.stem: Holding other factors constant, which change most likely increases a company's justified leading P/E?
options: A decrease in the dividend payout ratio with no change in growth
An increase in the required return on equity
An increase in the expected growth rate with no change in payout
questions.explanation: Justified P/E = payout/(r − g): higher g shrinks the denominator and raises P/E. A higher r lowers P/E; a lower payout with unchanged g lowers the numerator.

questions.stem: A company has a payout ratio of 50%, a required return of 9% and a sustainable growth rate of 5%. Its justified trailing P/E is closest to:
questions.explanation: Justified trailing P/E = payout × (1 + g)/(r − g) = 0.50 × 1.05/0.04 = 13.1. 12.5 is the leading P/E (0.50/0.04); 5.8 divides by r instead of r − g (0.525/0.09).

questions.stem: When computing a peer-group multiple, analysts often prefer the median to the arithmetic mean because the median:
options: adjusts automatically for differences in growth
is less affected by outliers
always produces a higher value estimate
questions.explanation: A few extreme multiples (e.g., P/E of 150 from near-zero EPS) can distort the mean; the median is robust to outliers. It does not systematically raise value or adjust for growth.

questions.stem: Company X trades at a forward P/E of 22 and its peers at a median of 16. X has higher expected earnings growth and lower risk than its peers. The most appropriate conclusion is that X:
options: is undervalued, because its P/E is above the median
is clearly overvalued relative to peers
may be fairly valued, because higher growth and lower risk justify a higher P/E
questions.explanation: A higher multiple is justified by higher growth and lower risk (justified P/E rises with g and falls with r). So the premium alone does not show overvaluation. A P/E above peers cannot by itself indicate undervaluation.

questions.stem: EV/EBITDA is often preferred to P/E when comparing companies that:
options: have very different levels of financial leverage
all have the same capital structure and tax rate
are financial institutions such as banks
questions.explanation: EV/EBITDA is a pre-interest, capital-structure-neutral measure, so it compares firms with different debt levels better than P/E. For banks, debt is an operating item and P/B or P/E is used instead.

flashcards.front: Method of comparables vs forecasted fundamentals
flashcards.back: Comparables: compare with peers' multiples (relative value). Fundamentals: compare with a justified multiple from a DCF model (intrinsic value).
(1 − b)/(r − g) = payout/(r − g).
(ROE − g)/(r − g); > 1 only when ROE > r.
Trailing uses last 12 months' EPS; forward (leading) uses next 12 months' expected EPS.
P/S (or EV/sales), because sales are positive when earnings are not.
EV = multiple × metric; equity = EV − debt − preferred − NCI + cash.

modules.title: Financial Statement Forecasting in Equity Valuation
modules.summary: Building and judging a forecast model: disaggregated revenue, margins and operating leverage, working capital, investment and financing, then turning model outputs into a value with probability-weighted scenarios.

acca.note: Not an ACCA syllabus item as such, though PM budgeting (sales volume × price, cost behaviour) and FR ratios (receivable/inventory/payable days) give a head start. The integrated three-statement model and probability-weighted scenarios are new.

lessons.title: Building the forecast model

cards.title: Why model the statements?
cards.body:
A valuation is only as good as its cash flow forecasts. A **three-statement model** forecasts the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement together, so the numbers stay consistent: profits feed equity, capex feeds PP&E, working capital feeds cash flow.

Models are **disaggregated**: revenue by segment, region or driver; costs split into fixed and variable. Each line should have a reason you can defend.

cards.title: Forecasting revenue
rows: Units sold × average selling price (e.g., airline: seats × load factor × yield)
Top-down: industry demand × company market share
Sum of segments, stores, products or customers

cards.title: Revenue and operating leverage
cards.body:
2.0M units at 50 = revenue 100M. Next year: units +6%, price +3%.
Revenue = 2.12M × 51.50 = **109.18M** (+9.18%).

Cost structure: fixed costs 40, variable 50% of revenue. Revenue 200 → EBIT = 200 − 40 − 100 = 60. Revenue +10% to 220 → EBIT = 220 − 40 − 110 = 70: **+16.7%**. Fixed costs magnify profit changes (operating leverage).

cards.title: Working capital from days
cards.formula:
Receivables = revenue × DSO ÷ 365
Inventory = COGS × DIO ÷ 365
Payables = COGS × DPO ÷ 365
cards.note: Revenue 365, DSO 40 → AR 40. COGS 219, DIO 60 → inventory 36; DPO 45 → payables 27.

cards.title: Investment and financing
cards.body:
- **Capex**: maintenance (≈ depreciation) plus growth capex, often linked to revenue (capex/sales or sales/PP&E).
- **Depreciation**: % of opening PP&E or by asset life.
- **Debt**: schedule of issues and repayments; interest often on **average** debt (creates a circular reference).
- **Dividends and buybacks**: per payout policy.
- **Balancing item**: cash or a revolving credit line makes the balance sheet balance.

lessons.title: Evaluating models and probability-weighted scenarios

cards.title: Evaluating a model
cards.body:
Checks a good analyst runs:
- **Mechanics**: balance sheet balances; cash flow ties to the change in cash; no hard-coded plugs.
- **Consistency**: growth matches reinvestment; margins consistent with strategy and competition.
- **Reasonableness**: compare forecasts with history and peers; returns on capital should fade toward the cost of capital over time.
- **Sensitivity**: which assumptions drive value (often revenue growth, margin, discount rate, terminal growth)?

cards.title: Probability-weighted value
cards.formula: V = Σ p_{s} × V_{s}
