cards.note: Build full models for each scenario (bear, base, bull), not just one-line tweaks.

cards.title: Scenario example
cards.body:
Bear 30 (25%), base 45 (50%), bull 65 (25%).
V = 0.25 × 30 + 0.50 × 45 + 0.25 × 65 = 7.5 + 22.5 + 16.25 = **46.25**

A simple average (equal weights) would give 46.67. Note the skew: upside (+20) exceeds downside (−15), so the weighted value sits above the base case.

cards.title: From model outputs to value
cards.body:
1. Forecast the explicit period (e.g., 5–10 years) until growth and returns stabilise.
2. Extract FCFF or FCFE (or dividends, or RI) from the model.
3. Estimate a **terminal value** (Gordon growth or exit multiple).
4. Discount at the matching rate (WACC or cost of equity).
5. Run scenarios and sensitivities; report a range, not just a point estimate.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Expect qualitative questions on judging a model: a forecast with ROIC staying far above WACC forever, revenue growing faster than the market for decades, or capex below depreciation while sales grow quickly are all **red flags**. Interest on average debt creates **circularity**; it is a feature, not an error.

questions.stem: A company sold 2.0 million units at 50 each. Next year, volume is forecast to rise 6% and price 3%. Forecast revenue is closest to:
options: 109.0 million
109.2 million
109.5 million
questions.explanation: Revenue = 2.0 × 1.06 × 50 × 1.03 = 2.12 × 51.50 = 109.18 million. 109.0 million adds the growth rates (9%) instead of compounding them (9.18%).

questions.stem: A company has fixed costs of 40 and variable costs equal to 50% of revenue. If revenue rises from 200 to 220, EBIT will increase by approximately:
questions.explanation: EBIT goes from 200 − 40 − 100 = 60 to 220 − 40 − 110 = 70, a 16.7% increase. EBIT grows faster than revenue (10%) because fixed costs do not rise. 20% would apply with fixed costs of 50.

questions.stem: Forecast revenue is 400 million and the analyst assumes days sales outstanding of 45. Forecast accounts receivable is closest to:
options: 49.3 million
180.0 million
8.9 million
questions.explanation: Receivables = revenue × DSO/365 = 400 × 45/365 = 49.3 million. 8.9 million divides 400 by 45; 180.0 million omits the division by 365 (400 × 45/100).

questions.stem: Debt is 100 at the start of the year and is forecast to be 140 at year-end. If the interest rate is 6% and the analyst computes interest on average debt, forecast interest expense is closest to:
questions.explanation: Average debt = (100 + 140)/2 = 120; interest = 6% × 120 = 7.2. 6.0 uses opening debt; 8.4 uses closing debt. Using average debt makes interest depend on the year's financing, creating a circular reference.

questions.stem: An analyst estimates values of 30 (bear, 25% probability), 45 (base, 50%) and 65 (bull, 25%). The probability-weighted value is closest to:
questions.explanation: V = 0.25 × 30 + 0.50 × 45 + 0.25 × 65 = 46.25. 45.00 is the base case alone; 46.67 is the equally weighted average.

questions.stem: Which forecast assumption is most likely a red flag in a long-term valuation model?
options: Return on invested capital staying far above the cost of capital indefinitely
Capital expenditure exceeding depreciation while revenue grows
Revenue growth fading toward nominal GDP growth
questions.explanation: Competition normally erodes excess returns, so ROIC should fade toward the cost of capital; keeping it far above forever overstates value. Fading growth and capex above depreciation for a growing firm are reasonable.

questions.stem: A sensitivity analysis is most useful for:
options: eliminating uncertainty from the value estimate
identifying which assumptions have the largest effect on value
ensuring the balance sheet balances
questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time to show which drivers (growth, margin, discount rate) move value most. It does not remove uncertainty; balance-sheet checks are a separate model-integrity test.

questions.stem: An analyst's model shows sales growing 15% a year for ten years while capital expenditure is set equal to 50% of depreciation. The most appropriate criticism is that:
options: the model is conservative, because low capex reduces free cash flow
the model is fine, because capex does not affect FCFF
the model is internally inconsistent, because rapid growth usually requires investment above depreciation
questions.explanation: Growth must be funded: rapid sales growth with capex below depreciation implies a shrinking asset base supporting much higher sales, which is inconsistent. Low capex actually raises forecast FCF (aggressive, not conservative), and capex is deducted in FCFF.

questions.stem: A company's revenue is 365 million and COGS is 219 million. The analyst assumes DSO of 40 days, DIO of 60 days and DPO of 45 days. Forecast net operating working capital (receivables + inventory − payables) is closest to:
options: 49 million
76 million
103 million
questions.explanation: Receivables = 365 × 40/365 = 40. Inventory = 219 × 60/365 = 36. Payables = 219 × 45/365 = 27. Net = 40 + 36 − 27 = 49 million. 76 million ignores payables; 103 million adds payables.

questions.stem: Compared with using only a single base-case forecast, a probability-weighted scenario approach is most likely to:
options: remove the need for a terminal value
capture asymmetric upside and downside outcomes in the value estimate
always produce a higher value
questions.explanation: Weighting several fully modelled scenarios reflects skewed outcomes (e.g., a large bull case or severe bear case). It still needs terminal values in each scenario and can raise or lower value depending on the skew.

questions.stem: In a top-down revenue forecast, an analyst is most likely to start with:
options: the company's order backlog by customer
each store's sales history
industry market size and the company's expected market share
questions.explanation: Top-down starts from the macro or industry level (market size, GDP) and applies the company's share. Store-level and customer-level data are bottom-up inputs.

flashcards.back: Integrated forecast of income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement; profits, capex and working capital link the three.
AR = revenue × DSO/365. Inventory = COGS × DIO/365. Payables = COGS × DPO/365.
Fixed costs make EBIT change by a larger % than revenue.
V = Σ p_{s} × V_{s}; probabilities sum to 1.
More accurate but creates a circular reference (interest → net income → cash → debt).
ROIC ≫ WACC forever; growth without reinvestment; capex < depreciation while growing fast; margins far above peers without reason.
Top-down: macro/industry → company share. Bottom-up: segments, products, stores, customers summed up.

modules.title: Industry and Competitive Analysis
modules.summary: Why industry matters for valuation: classifying companies, sizing an industry and its growth, profitability and concentration (CR and HHI), and using Porter's Five Forces and PESTLE to support a valuation narrative.

acca.note: BT and SBL covered Porter's Five Forces, PESTEL and the industry life cycle as strategy tools. New for CFA: classification systems (GICS, ICB, RBICS), concentration measures, and explicitly linking each force to margins, growth and therefore valuation inputs.

lessons.title: Classification, size, growth and concentration

cards.title: Why industry analysis?
cards.body:
Industry conditions explain much of a company's growth and profitability. Analysts use industry work to: set revenue growth and margin assumptions, choose peers for multiples, judge how long excess returns can last, and spot threats.

Process: define the industry → size and growth → profitability and structure → competitive forces and external factors → implications for the company's forecasts.

cards.title: Classification systems
rows: Very granular; multi-segment firms mapped by revenue

cards.title: Concentration measures
cards.formula:
CR_{n} = sum of the n largest market shares
HHI = Σ (market share in %)^{2}
cards.note: HHI ranges up to 10,000 (monopoly). Roughly: < 1,500 unconcentrated; 1,500–2,500 moderately; > 2,500 highly concentrated (older US guidelines; the 2023 US guidelines use 1,000 and 1,800).

cards.title: Size, growth and share trends
cards.body:
- **Size**: total revenue of the industry (the market the company addresses).
- **Growth**: historical and forecast; cyclical vs defensive vs growth industries; life-cycle stage (embryonic, growth, shakeout, mature, decline).
- **Share trends**: is the company gaining or losing share?

Company revenue growth ≈ (1 + market growth)(1 + share change) − 1. Market 50bn growing 4%, share 12% → 13%: revenue 6.0bn → 6.76bn (+12.7%).

lessons.title: Five Forces, PESTLE and valuation

cards.title: Porter's Five Forces → valuation
rows: Many similar firms, high fixed costs, slow growth

cards.title: PESTLE
rows: Carbon pricing, climate risk, resource scarcity

cards.title: Linking analysis to the model
cards.body:
Five Forces and PESTLE are only useful if they change a number:
- Strong barriers and weak buyers → higher sustainable margins, longer competitive advantage period.
- New regulation → higher costs or capex.
- Technological substitution → lower long-run growth or terminal value.

A valuation **narrative** ties the story (industry position) to the inputs (growth, margins, reinvestment, risk).

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: You already know Five Forces and PESTEL from BT/SBL. CFA spells it PESTLE and, more importantly, asks **what each force does to valuation inputs**. It also tests concentration maths (CR, HHI) and classification systems, which ACCA did not cover.

questions.stem: An industry has five firms with market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, 10% and 10%. Its Herfindahl–Hirschman Index is closest to:
The Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) assigns a company to a sub-industry mainly on the basis of its:
options: country of incorporation
principal business activity, primarily revenue
share price volatility
questions.explanation: GICS classifies companies by principal business activity, mainly measured by revenue (with earnings and market perception as secondary inputs). Volatility and domicile are not classification criteria.

questions.stem: An industry's revenue of 50 billion is expected to grow 4% next year, and a company's market share is expected to rise from 12% to 13%. The company's revenue growth is closest to:
questions.explanation: Revenue goes from 0.12 × 50 = 6.0 to 0.13 × 52 = 6.76 billion: growth = 12.7%. 8.3% is the share gain alone (13/12 − 1); 5.0% adds 4% and 1 percentage point.

questions.stem: In the industry life cycle, a stage marked by slowing growth, falling prices, excess capacity and consolidation is best described as:
options: shakeout
growth
embryonic
questions.explanation: Shakeout follows the growth stage: demand growth slows, competition intensifies, weaker firms exit and the industry consolidates. Embryonic and growth stages feature rising demand and less price pressure.

questions.stem: An industry where a few large customers buy most of the output and can easily switch between suppliers is most likely to have:
options: low rivalry and high pricing power
high buyer power and lower margins
high supplier power and higher margins
questions.explanation: Concentrated buyers with low switching costs can push prices down, so buyer power is high and margins suffer. The other options describe the reverse.

questions.stem: A government announces a carbon tax on cement production. In a PESTLE framework this is best classified as a(n):
options: technological factor
social factor
environmental (and political/legal) factor affecting costs
questions.explanation: A carbon tax arises from environmental concerns and is implemented through policy and law; for valuation it raises costs and may cut margins. It is not a social or technological factor.

questions.stem: High barriers to entry in an industry will most likely lead an analyst to forecast:
options: a longer period of above-normal margins and ROIC
greater threat of substitutes
faster fading of excess returns toward the cost of capital
questions.explanation: Barriers protect incumbents from new competitors, so excess returns can persist longer. Low barriers cause faster fading. Substitute threat is a separate force.

questions.stem: Firms in an industry have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, 10% and 10%. If the two smallest firms merge, the change in the industry's HHI is closest to:
questions.explanation: Before: 2,450. After: 35^{2} + 25^{2} + 20^{2} + 20^{2} = 2,650, so ΔHHI = +200 (equal to 2 × 10 × 10). +400 is the new firm's squared share (20^{2}); +100 is one firm's squared share.

questions.stem: Which industry characteristic most likely leads to intense rivalry?
options: Strong brand loyalty and patents
Rapid industry growth with few competitors
High fixed costs, slow industry growth and undifferentiated products
questions.explanation: High fixed costs push firms to cut prices to fill capacity, slow growth makes gains come from rivals, and commodity products compete on price. Brands, patents and rapid growth reduce rivalry.

questions.stem: A company sells both medical devices and consumer cosmetics. Under a revenue-based classification system, it will most likely be classified according to:
options: the segment that generates most of its revenue
the segment with the highest growth rate
its country of listing
questions.explanation: Systems such as GICS and ICB classify by primary source of revenue, so the larger segment determines the classification. Growth and listing venue are not the basis.

questions.stem: Linking industry analysis to valuation, a credible threat of substitute products is most likely to cause an analyst to lower the company's:
options: number of shares outstanding
forecast pricing power and long-run margins
cost of debt
questions.explanation: Close substitutes cap the price a company can charge, reducing margin and growth assumptions. Financing costs and share count are not directly affected.

flashcards.back: Sum of the market shares of the n largest firms.
Σ (market share %)^{2}; max 10,000. > 2,500 = highly concentrated (older US guideline; 2023 US guidelines: > 1,800).

flashcards.front: ΔHHI from a merger of firms with shares a and b
flashcards.back: 2 × a × b (in % points).
Sector → industry group → industry → sub-industry; based on principal business activity (revenue).
New entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power, rivalry.
Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental.
Embryonic → growth → shakeout → mature → decline.

modules.title: Company Analysis: Past, Present, and Future
modules.summary: Analysing a company's competitive strategy and position, its revenue drivers and pricing power, operating profitability, working capital, capital investment and capital structure, and turning that history into forecasts.

acca.note: SBL covered generic strategies and competitive advantage; FR covered ratio analysis (margins, working capital days, gearing). New for CFA: tying strategy to measurable revenue drivers, pricing power, ROIC vs WACC, and using the analysis to forecast.

lessons.title: Competitive position, revenue drivers and pricing power

cards.title: Competitive strategies
rows: What to look for in the numbers
Low prices, high volume, high asset turnover, thin but stable margins
Unique product customers pay more for
Premium prices, high gross margin, high R&D/marketing spend
Serves a niche with cost or differentiation
Strong position in a narrow segment

cards.title: Revenue drivers
cards.body:
Break revenue into drivers you can forecast and check:
- Retail: stores × sales per store (same-store growth + new stores)
- Subscription: subscribers × ARPU (2M × 120 = 240M), with churn
- Airline: capacity (seat-km) × load factor × yield
- Pharma: patients × price × market share, minus patent expiries

Split growth into **volume** and **price/mix**: price-driven growth is often less durable.

cards.title: Pricing power
cards.body:
A firm has **pricing power** if it can raise prices without losing much volume (low price elasticity). Signs: stable or rising gross margins when input costs rise, few substitutes, strong brands, switching costs, network effects.

Example: revenue 100, COGS 60 (GM 40%). A 5% price rise with no volume loss: GM = 45 ÷ 105 = **42.9%**. Firms without pricing power see margins squeezed when costs rise.

cards.title: Sources of durable advantage (moats)
cards.body:
- Intangibles: brands, patents, licences
- Switching costs
- Network effects
- Cost advantages: scale, process, location
- Efficient scale in a niche market

The longer the advantage lasts, the longer ROIC can stay above WACC, and the higher the value.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: SBL taught generic strategies qualitatively. CFA expects you to **see the strategy in the financials**: a cost leader with falling margins, or a "premium" brand whose gross margin trails peers, is a contradiction worth flagging.

lessons.title: Profitability, working capital, capex and capital structure

cards.title: Return on invested capital
cards.formula:
ROIC = NOPAT ÷ invested capital
NOPAT = EBIT × (1 − t)
where: net operating assets = debt + equity − excess cash (or operating WC + net PP&E + intangibles)
cards.note: Value is created when ROIC > WACC. EBIT 200, t 25%, IC 1,000 → ROIC 15%; with WACC 9% the firm creates value.

cards.title: Operating profitability
cards.body:
Look at **gross**, **EBIT** and **EBITDA margins** over time and vs peers. Separate costs into fixed and variable to understand **operating leverage**: high fixed costs mean profits swing more with revenue.

Ask why margins changed: price, mix, input costs, scale, or one-offs.

cards.title: Working capital
cards.formula: Cash conversion cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO
cards.note: DSO 45 + DIO 70 − DPO 50 = 65 days. A rising CCC ties up cash; a negative CCC (e.g., some retailers, subscription firms) means suppliers or customers fund the business.

cards.title: Capex and capital structure
cards.body:
- **Capex**: maintenance (keep capacity) vs growth (add capacity). Compare capex with depreciation and revenue growth; capex/depreciation > 1 for a growing firm is normal.
- **Capital structure**: debt level and maturity, interest coverage, net debt/EBITDA (debt 900 − cash 150 = 750; ÷ EBITDA 300 = 2.5×).
- Leverage magnifies ROE but adds financial risk and raises the cost of equity.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Past → present → future: use history to understand drivers, check whether the present strategy changes them, then forecast. A firm with ROIC below WACC destroys value by growing; faster growth only helps if ROIC > WACC.

questions.stem: A company sells a commodity product at the lowest prices in its industry, runs large-scale facilities and reports thin but stable margins with high asset turnover. Its strategy is best described as:
options: focus
differentiation
cost leadership
questions.explanation: Low prices, scale and high asset turnover with thin margins are hallmarks of cost leadership. Differentiation shows up as premium prices and high gross margins; focus targets a narrow niche.

questions.stem: A company with revenue of 100 and COGS of 60 raises prices by 5% with no loss of volume and no change in unit costs. Its new gross margin is closest to:
questions.explanation: New revenue = 105; COGS = 60; gross profit = 45; margin = 45/105 = 42.9%. 40.0% is the old margin; 45.0% divides by the old revenue.

questions.stem: Which evidence most strongly suggests a company has pricing power?
options: It has the largest number of employees in its industry
It maintained gross margins while input costs rose sharply
Its revenue rose because it cut prices to win volume
questions.explanation: Passing higher input costs on to customers without margin erosion shows pricing power. Price cuts to win volume suggest the opposite; headcount says nothing about pricing power.

questions.stem: A streaming service has 2 million subscribers paying an average of 120 a year. Annual revenue is closest to:
options: 60 million
122 million
240 million
questions.explanation: Revenue = subscribers × ARPU = 2 million × 120 = 240 million. 122 million adds the two inputs; 60 million divides instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A company has EBIT of 200, a tax rate of 25% and invested capital of 1,000. Its WACC is 9%. Which statement is most accurate?
options: ROIC is 15% and the firm creates value
ROIC is 15% and the firm destroys value
ROIC is 20% and the firm creates value
questions.explanation: ROIC = NOPAT/IC = 200 × 0.75/1,000 = 15%. Since 15% > 9% WACC, the firm creates value. 20% uses pre-tax EBIT.

questions.stem: A company has DSO of 45 days, DIO of 70 days and DPO of 50 days. Its cash conversion cycle is closest to:
options: 25 days
65 days
165 days
questions.explanation: CCC = DSO + DIO − DPO = 45 + 70 − 50 = 65 days. 165 adds DPO; 25 subtracts DIO instead of adding it (45 − 70 + 50).

questions.stem: A company earns an ROIC of 7% and has a WACC of 9%. If it doubles its growth rate by reinvesting more, its value will most likely:
options: be unchanged, because growth does not affect value
increase, because growth always adds value
decrease, because each reinvested unit earns less than its cost of capital
questions.explanation: When ROIC < WACC, every unit invested earns less than investors require, so faster growth destroys more value. Growth adds value only when ROIC exceeds WACC.

questions.stem: A company has debt of 900, cash of 150 and EBITDA of 300. Its net debt/EBITDA ratio is closest to:
questions.explanation: Net debt = 900 − 150 = 750; 750/300 = 2.5×. 3.0× uses gross debt; 3.5× adds cash to debt.

questions.stem: A retailer has a negative cash conversion cycle. This most likely means that:
options: its inventory turns over very slowly
its suppliers are effectively financing its working capital
it is in financial distress
questions.explanation: A negative CCC means the retailer collects from customers and sells inventory before paying suppliers, so suppliers fund operations. It is a strength, not a distress signal, and implies fast inventory turnover.

questions.stem: A company claims a differentiation strategy based on its premium brand, yet its gross margin is consistently below that of its peers. The analyst should most likely:
options: conclude the company is a cost leader
accept the claim, as gross margin is unrelated to strategy
question whether the company really has pricing power from its brand
questions.explanation: Differentiation should show up as premium pricing and above-peer gross margins. Below-peer margins contradict the claimed strategy and question its pricing power. Low margins alone do not make it a cost leader.

questions.stem: Which is the best indicator that a company's capital spending is mainly for growth rather than maintenance?
options: Capex well above depreciation alongside rising capacity and revenue
Capex well below depreciation
Capex roughly equal to depreciation with flat revenue
questions.explanation: Capex well above depreciation, with capacity and sales rising, indicates expansion. Capex ≈ depreciation with flat sales is maintenance; capex below depreciation implies a shrinking asset base.

flashcards.back: Cost leadership, differentiation, focus (cost or differentiation in a niche).
Ability to raise prices without losing much volume; evidence: stable gross margins when input costs rise.
NOPAT/invested capital; value created only when ROIC > WACC.
DSO + DIO − DPO.
Maintenance keeps existing capacity (≈ depreciation); growth capex adds capacity.
(Debt − cash) ÷ EBITDA; common leverage measure.
Intangibles, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, efficient scale.

modules.title: Equity Analyst Research Reports
modules.summary: What goes into an equity research report, how initiation-of-coverage and update reports differ, sell-side vs buy-side research, why analysts' value estimates differ, and how to treat reports from activist short sellers.

acca.note: Not covered by ACCA. Report-writing skills from SBL help with structure, but the content (ratings, target prices, sell-side conflicts, activist short reports) is new.

lessons.title: Elements of a research report; sell-side vs buy-side

cards.title: Typical report elements
rows: Recommendation (rating), target price, key thesis in a few lines
Why the market is mispricing the stock; catalysts
Business model, competitive position, industry drivers
What could make the thesis wrong
Conflicts of interest, rating definitions, holdings

cards.title: Initiation vs update reports
cards.body:
An **initiation of coverage** report is the first full report on a company: long and comprehensive, with the business model, industry, full model and valuation.

**Update** (or flash) reports are short: they react to earnings, news or guidance and say whether the thesis, forecasts, rating or target price change.

cards.title: Sell-side vs buy-side
rows: Brokers, investment banks, independent research firms
Asset managers, pension funds, hedge funds
Recommendation to buy, hold, size or sell in a portfolio
Investment banking ties, access to management
Fewer external; career and portfolio pressures

cards.title: Target price and expected return
cards.body:
Price 50, 12-month target price 60, expected dividend 1.00.
Expected total return = (60 − 50 + 1) ÷ 50 = **22%**.

Whether that earns a "buy" depends on the firm's rating definitions, e.g., expected return above the required return (or the market) by some margin.

lessons.title: Why value estimates differ; activist short sellers

cards.title: Why analysts disagree
cards.body:
Two competent analysts can value the same stock very differently because of:
- **Forecasts**: revenue growth, margins, reinvestment
- **Discount rate**: beta, equity risk premium, risk-free rate
- **Terminal value**: long-run growth or exit multiple
- **Model choice**: DDM vs FCF vs multiples
- **Scenario weights**
- **Time horizon** of the target price

Good reports make assumptions explicit and show sensitivity tables, so readers can see what drives the gap.

cards.title: Activist short sellers
cards.body:
**Activist short sellers** take a short position and then publish a report arguing the stock is overvalued, often alleging accounting problems, fraud or an unsustainable business model.

They can expose real wrongdoing, but they profit if the price falls, so they have a clear incentive. Analysts should evaluate the evidence independently, check the company's response and audited filings, and avoid both automatic dismissal and panic.

cards.title: Using reports well
cards.body:
When reading a report, ask:
- Are assumptions consistent with industry analysis and history?
- Is the rating consistent with the target price and stated rating definitions?
- What are the conflicts of interest?
- What would make the thesis wrong, and is that risk priced in?

Sell-side ratings skew toward "buy"; a "hold" can be a polite negative.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Expect qualitative questions: which element belongs in which section, which conflicts affect sell-side analysts, why an initiation differs from an update, and how to respond to an activist short report. Link to Ethics: independence and objectivity (Standard I(B)) and reasonable basis (V(A)).

questions.stem: A comprehensive first report on a company, including a business description, industry analysis, full financial model and valuation, is best described as a(n):
options: earnings preview note
initiation of coverage report
flash update
questions.explanation: The initiation of coverage is the analyst's first and most detailed report on a company. Flash updates and earnings previews are short, event-driven notes.

questions.stem: Compared with a buy-side analyst, a sell-side analyst most likely:
options: makes recommendations only to internal portfolio managers
faces no potential conflict from investment banking relationships
publishes ratings and target prices for external clients
questions.explanation: Sell-side analysts at brokers and banks publish ratings and target prices for clients and can face investment-banking conflicts. Recommending only to internal portfolio managers describes the buy-side.

questions.stem: A share trades at 50. An analyst's 12-month target price is 60, and a dividend of 1.00 is expected. The expected total return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Expected return = (60 − 50 + 1)/50 = 22%. 20% ignores the dividend; 18% subtracts it.

questions.stem: In a research report, a discussion of what could cause the investment thesis to fail most likely appears in the:
options: summary of the business model
risks section
disclosures section
questions.explanation: The risks section sets out what could make the thesis or valuation wrong. Disclosures cover conflicts and rating definitions; the business description explains how the company makes money.

questions.stem: Two analysts use the same DCF model structure for a company but reach very different values. The most likely explanation is differences in their:
options: share count, since it is subjective
accounting standards
assumptions for growth, margins, discount rate and terminal value
questions.explanation: Value estimates are highly sensitive to forecast and discount-rate assumptions, especially terminal growth. The accounting standards are the company's, not the analyst's, and the share count is a fact.

questions.stem: An activist short seller publishes a report alleging that a company inflates revenue. An analyst covering the company should most appropriately:
options: independently assess the evidence and the company's response before revising views
immediately cut the rating to sell to protect clients
dismiss the report because the short seller profits if the price falls
questions.explanation: The short seller's incentive does not make the allegations false or true. The analyst should test the claims against filings and evidence and weigh the company's response, consistent with having a reasonable basis for any recommendation.

questions.stem: A sensitivity table in a research report most likely shows:
options: the analyst's personal holdings in the stock
how the value estimate changes with key assumptions such as growth and discount rate
the company's historical share price
questions.explanation: Sensitivity tables vary key inputs (e.g., WACC and terminal growth) to show the range of values and which assumptions matter most. Holdings belong in disclosures; price history is background.

questions.stem: Which is most likely a conflict of interest specific to sell-side research?
options: Pressure to recommend stocks already held in the analyst's own fund
Lack of access to public filings
Pressure to issue favourable ratings on companies that are investment-banking clients
questions.explanation: Sell-side analysts work for firms that earn fees from issuers, which can pressure them toward favourable ratings. Recommending stocks held in one's own fund is more a buy-side issue; public filings are available to all.

questions.stem: An update report published after quarterly earnings would most likely:
options: state whether forecasts, rating or target price have changed in light of the results
be longer than the initiation of coverage report
repeat the full business description and industry analysis
questions.explanation: Update reports focus on what has changed: results versus expectations and any revisions to forecasts, rating or target price. Full descriptions belong in the initiation, which is the longer report.

questions.stem: An analyst's base-case value is 48 with a current price of 50, but her bull case (30% probability) is 75 and her bear case (20% probability) is 30, with the base case at 50% probability. Her probability-weighted value is closest to:
questions.explanation: Weighted value = 0.30 × 75 + 0.50 × 48 + 0.20 × 30 = 22.5 + 24 + 6 = 52.50, above the price of 50, because upside is larger and more likely than downside. 48.00 is the base case alone; 51.00 weights the three scenarios equally.

questions.stem: A broker defines "buy" as an expected 12-month total return above 15%. An analyst's report shows a price of 40, a target price of 49 and an expected dividend of 1.00, but rates the stock "hold". The most appropriate conclusion is that:
options: the target price must be wrong because it exceeds the current price
the rating is consistent with the target price
the rating appears inconsistent with the target price and the broker's rating definitions
questions.explanation: Expected return = (49 − 40 + 1)/40 = 25%, above the 15% buy threshold, so a hold rating conflicts with the analyst's own target and the stated definitions. A target above the current price is normal for a positive view.

questions.stem: A 12-month target price in a sell-side report is best described as the analyst's estimate of:
options: where the share price should trade at the end of the stated horizon
the share's book value per share in 12 months
the price at which the company will repurchase shares
questions.explanation: A target price is the analyst's projected share price at a specified horizon, usually 12 months, based on the valuation. It is neither a buyback price nor a book value forecast.

flashcards.front: Key elements of an equity research report
flashcards.back: Summary (rating, target price), thesis, business and industry, financial forecasts, valuation, risks, ESG/governance, disclosures.
Initiation: first, comprehensive report. Update: short, event-driven, states changes to forecasts/rating/target.
Sell-side: brokers/banks, published ratings and targets for clients. Buy-side: asset managers, internal recommendations.

flashcards.front: Expected return from a target price
flashcards.back: (Target − price + expected dividends) ÷ price.
Shorts a stock, then publishes a negative report; may expose problems but has an incentive for the price to fall.
Different forecasts, discount rates, terminal assumptions, model choice, scenario weights and horizons.

modules.title: The Capital Asset Pricing Model, Market Model, and Other Factor-Based Equity Models
modules.summary: Estimating the required return on equity: CAPM, estimating beta with a market-model regression on real return data (and the choices that involves), and multifactor models such as APT and Fama–French.

acca.note: FM applied CAPM with a given beta to find the cost of equity; AFM added portfolio theory. New for CFA: estimating beta yourself by regression (window, frequency, index choice, adjusted beta), interpreting regression output, and multifactor/APT models.

lessons.title: CAPM and estimating beta by regression

cards.title: Market model and beta
cards.note: β is the slope of a regression of the stock's returns on the market's (often excess returns). ρ 0.6, σ_{i} 30%, σ_{m} 15% → β = 0.6 × 30 ÷ 15 = 1.2.

cards.title: Regression on the calculator
cards.body:
Monthly returns (%): market 2, −1, 3, 0, 1; stock 3.1, −1.4, 3.9, 0.2, 1.7.

Slope (β) = **1.35**, intercept (α) = **0.15%** a month, R^{2} ≈ 0.99 (unrealistically high: real stocks show R^{2} of roughly 0.1–0.5).

cards.title: Estimation choices
rows: Longer = more data but stale beta
Daily data suffers from non-trading/thin trading
Raw returns give similar slope if R_{f} is stable

cards.title: Adjusted beta and interpretation
cards.body:
Estimated betas tend to **mean-revert toward 1**. A common (Blume) adjustment:
Adjusted β = 2/3 × raw β + 1/3 × 1.0
Raw 1.5 → adjusted **1.33**.

R^{2} = share of the stock's return variance explained by the market (systematic); 1 − R^{2} is diversifiable (idiosyncratic). The intercept α is the average return not explained by the market; when the regression uses excess returns it is Jensen's alpha.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: In FM beta was given. CFA expects you to **estimate** it: choose window, frequency and index, read slope, intercept, R^{2} and standard error, and adjust raw beta. Also: CFA writes E(R_{m}) − R_{f} as the equity risk premium, which FM called the market risk premium.

lessons.title: APT and multifactor models

cards.title: Why more than one factor?
cards.body:
CAPM says only market beta is priced. In practice, other characteristics help explain returns: **size** (small caps), **value** (high book-to-market), **momentum**, **profitability**, **investment**, **liquidity**.

Multifactor models give a richer cost of equity and a better benchmark for judging performance.

cards.title: Arbitrage pricing theory (APT)
cards.note: R_{f} 3%; β_{1} 1.2, λ_{1} 4%; β_{2} 0.5, λ_{2} 2% → 3 + 4.8 + 1.0 = 8.8%. APT assumes no arbitrage; it does not say which factors.

cards.title: Fama–French three-factor model
cards.formula: R_{i} − R_{f} = α + b_{m}(R_{m} − R_{f}) + s × SMB + h × HML + ε
cards.note: Carhart adds momentum (WML); Pastor–Stambaugh adds liquidity.

cards.title: Fama–French cost of equity
cards.body:
R_{f} 3%, market premium 5%, SMB premium 2%, HML premium 3%.
Loadings: b_{m} 1.1, s 0.4, h −0.3.

E(R) = 3 + 1.1 × 5 + 0.4 × 2 − 0.3 × 3 = 3 + 5.5 + 0.8 − 0.9 = **8.4%**

Positive s → small-cap tilt. Negative h → growth (low book-to-market) tilt, which lowers the required return here.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: A negative factor loading is not an error: it means the stock behaves like the opposite side of that factor (e.g., h < 0 → growth stock). And the factor **premium** (λ) is not the same as the **loading** (β): multiply them.

questions.stem: The risk-free rate is 3.5%, the equity risk premium is 5.5% and a stock's beta is 1.2. Its required return under the CAPM is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(R) = 3.5% + 1.2 × 5.5% = 10.1%. 6.6% omits the risk-free rate; 14.3% treats 9% (3.5% + 5.5%) as the market return and multiplies it by beta (3.5% + 1.2 × 9%).

questions.stem: A stock's returns have a correlation of 0.6 with the market. The stock's standard deviation is 30% and the market's is 15%. The stock's beta is closest to:
questions.explanation: β = ρ × σ_{i}/σ_{m} = 0.6 × 30/15 = 1.2. 2.0 omits the correlation; 0.3 inverts the volatility ratio (0.6 × 15/30).

questions.stem: A raw regression beta is 1.5. Using the adjustment adjusted β = 2/3 × raw β + 1/3 × 1.0, the adjusted beta is closest to:
questions.explanation: Adjusted β = 2/3 × 1.5 + 1/3 × 1.0 = 1.0 + 0.333 = 1.33. The adjustment pulls betas toward 1 because estimated betas tend to mean-revert. 1.50 is the raw beta.

questions.stem: A market-model regression of a stock's monthly excess returns on the market's excess returns gives an intercept of 0.20%, a slope of 0.85 and an R^{2} of 0.40. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The stock's beta is 0.20
40% of the variation in the stock's excess returns is explained by the market
60% of the stock's risk is systematic
questions.explanation: The slope (0.85) is beta; the intercept (0.20%) is alpha. R^{2} = 0.40 means 40% of the variance is explained by the market (systematic); the other 60% is idiosyncratic.

questions.stem: An analyst estimating beta prefers weekly or monthly returns over daily returns mainly because daily returns:
options: always produce a beta of exactly 1
are not available for most stocks
can be distorted by non-synchronous or thin trading
questions.explanation: For less liquid stocks, daily prices may not reflect market moves on the same day, biasing beta (usually downward). Daily data are widely available and do not force beta to 1.

questions.stem: Under a two-factor APT model, the risk-free rate is 3%, factor 1 has a premium of 4% and factor 2 a premium of 2%. A stock has sensitivities of 1.2 to factor 1 and 0.5 to factor 2. Its expected return is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(R) = 3% + 1.2 × 4% + 0.5 × 2% = 3 + 4.8 + 1.0 = 8.8%. 7.8% omits the second factor; 9.0% adds the unweighted premiums (3 + 4 + 2).

questions.stem: Using the Fama–French three-factor model: R_{f} = 3%, market premium = 5%, SMB premium = 2%, HML premium = 3%. A stock has b_{m} = 1.1, s = 0.4 and h = −0.3. Its required return is closest to:
A stock has a significant negative loading on the HML factor. This most likely indicates that the stock:
options: behaves like a small-cap stock
has no exposure to the market factor
behaves like a growth (low book-to-market) stock
questions.explanation: HML is long high book-to-market (value) and short low book-to-market (growth). A negative loading means the stock moves like growth stocks. Size exposure is captured by SMB; market exposure by b_{m}.

questions.stem: A fund earned 12% when the risk-free rate was 3% and the market returned 10%. The fund's beta is 1.2. Its Jensen's alpha is closest to:
questions.explanation: Expected return = 3% + 1.2 × (10% − 3%) = 11.4%. Alpha = 12% − 11.4% = 0.6%. 2.0% compares with the market return (12 − 10) and ignores beta; −0.6% reverses the subtraction (11.4 − 12).

questions.stem: Changing the market proxy from a domestic index to a global index when estimating beta will most likely:
options: leave beta unchanged, because beta is a fixed property of the stock
change the beta estimate, because beta is measured relative to the chosen index
always increase the beta
questions.explanation: Beta is the covariance with the chosen benchmark divided by its variance, so a different index gives a different estimate. The direction is not always up.

questions.stem: Compared with the CAPM, a key difference of the arbitrage pricing theory is that APT:
options: assumes all investors hold the same portfolio of risky assets
requires the market portfolio to be mean–variance efficient
allows several systematic risk factors and does not specify which ones
questions.explanation: APT relies on no-arbitrage and a linear factor structure with multiple priced factors, without naming them. Market-portfolio efficiency and identical portfolios are CAPM assumptions.

questions.stem: Using the market model, a stock has α = 0.1% and β = 1.3 (monthly). If the market returns 2% in a month, the stock's expected return for that month is closest to:
questions.explanation: E(R_{i}) = α + β × R_{m} = 0.1% + 1.3 × 2% = 2.7%. 2.6% omits alpha; 2.1% adds alpha to the market return without beta.

flashcards.back: R_{i} = α_{i} + β_{i}R_{m} + ε_{i}; β is the regression slope.
β = Cov(R_{i}, R_{m})/Var(R_{m}) = ρσ_{i}/σ_{m}.
2/3 × raw β + 1/3 × 1.0 (betas mean-revert toward 1).
Share of return variance explained by the market (systematic); 1 − R^{2} is idiosyncratic.
E(R_{i}) = R_{f} + Σ β_{i,k}λ_{k}; multiple priced factors, not specified; no-arbitrage.
R_{i} − R_{f} = α + b_{m}(R_{m} − R_{f}) + s·SMB + h·HML. Carhart adds momentum.
Actual return − [R_{f} + β(R_{m} − R_{f})].
